                                                                6
                    INTRODUCTION BY AMELIA WHYMAN
My name is Amelia Whyman, I’m 17 years old. I’m a proud Malyangapa and Wankumarra
woman. I grew up in a small regional town called Wilcanna, in far Western NSW, where I
dance with the Barkinji Baaka dance group and speak up as a young leader for my
community and surrounds as a voice to empower future generations. I moved to Sydney
to build connections and get my voice out there to be more known. I started doing dance
with a well known dance group called ‘Bujja Bujja butterfly Dancers’. I’m working as a
Youth Ambassador with Mounty Aboriginal Youth and Community Services, building an
Aboriginal Youth Peak for NSW, so young people can have more of a voice in decisions
that affect their lives and have a place to be themselves.

What racism have you seen or experienced?
I came to Sydney from Wilcannia in search of better education opportunities that aren’t
available in my hometown. I started at a boarding school in Sydney. I would say there’s a
big racism problem within the boarding community at the school but also throughout all
schools. When I started there, there were problems with feeling culturally involved. It’s
the same for other students. Issues came up for First Nations students in the boarding
house where it’s supposed to be home away from home. How can they feel comfortable
there? It gets hard for them.

I have had racist run-ins. While I was waiting at [the station], this man walked past me,
and he sat this piece of paper on the pole in front of me. This is my spot, this is my paper,
he was calling me the N word, and racially profiling me. That guy was still slinging racial
words to me, while I was walking off. I was only 15 years old. The bystanders all just
watched. It made me feel like shit. I gave him the rude finger while walking off.

What do you do about racism?
I’m one of those people who will call racism out as it happens - if I can. Sometimes I call
it out, and sometimes I don’t because I get really scared. Even online.

It’s not always worth taking someone on who is a racist, you can’t really change their
thoughts. It can bring back all that trauma from generations - because stories get passed
down, especially the racist incidents. You can experience pain that is passed down from
your ancestors, you can get scared for your cultural safety, for your physical safety - you
feel it.

Sometimes when I’m doing cultural dance I feel a bit judged, people whisper. We might
not say anything while we’re dancing as it’s about culture. Other times we have to call it
out.

You can see when you should call it out. Sometimes you know culturally or spiritually
that people need to be called out.


                                             7
My ancestors connect to me spiritually. There have been so many things over the years
that we as First Nations people weren’t allowed to do, through the stolen generations
and other racist policies. We couldn’t stand up back then but you can now. Sometimes
my ancestors will say this isn’t a safe space for you. Other times they’re saying you
should stand your ground.

A fair few adults and young people want to take action against racism. But some people
would be scared or clueless about how to do it. Some people will walk away and some
people will stand up because they won’t let anyone talk about their culture, others will
go the legal route. A lot of people don’t know the ways to go about it legally - and how they
can get help and handle it.

I help other young people with racism. If they contact me for help, I do some thinking,
then I talk to them and plan with them. So they don’t get in more trouble in how they
respond to racism – whether that happens in their community, in public spaces or
wherever.

At the school I just graduated from, a lot of the girls look up to me as a big sister or leader,
and when they have problems they get in touch with me and ask for advice and guidance.
A fair bit of the advice I give is about racism and how to solve it without making a bigger
problem. They are only young and I talk to them like I am their big sister. I have five
younger siblings. I help them understand the things they can and can’t do and how they
can work around issues to make it a more comfortable space, especially while boarding
at school.

While I was still at school I saw a young First Nations girl in Year 8 standing there crying
and talking to a teacher who wasn’t First Nations. I asked if she was okay. She said she
felt culturally unsafe, uncomfortable and that the school was ‘whitewashed’. I come
from a very cultural community so I knew how she felt. I gave her some support. I didn’t
walk past. I stopped and helped her with her feelings. She liked that I was talking to her,
rather than the teacher. She didn’t feel so alone. It was that connection with me that was
important.

Also, calling racism out is sometimes effective and sometimes not. When we
complained before about racism at school the principal didn’t do much about it. I think
they were blindsided by their relationships with the staff we were complaining about. But
when we have good leadership, like now, I encourage the other students to write down
when something happens. When you feel culturally unsafe, then take it to the principal.
She will listen.

How does racism affect young people?
Racism can affect the mindset of young people and how they see the world. A kid can
grow up in a happy family and then they experience racism and they get confused about
their place in the world. You don’t feel a sense of community. You feel isolated.

                                               8
Everyone has been told about it. But it affects everyone differently when you experience
it.

It can make some people get depressed and separate themselves from society. It can
lead to people feeling like suicide. It can affect their mental state, their physical state -
stop them from eating, drinking - to get skinny, sick.

What needs to be done about racism?
The solutions can come through culture and from First Nations people themselves, but
everyone has a role in addressing racism, recognising and responding to it. Everyone
needs to have an understanding of racism and its effects.

Sometimes at school they do Koori lunch meetings, there’s cultural dancing too, but
there is really nothing else for First Nations students and after these activities, they go
back into a school community where they don’t feel culturally safe. In communities we
exchange cultural stories, learn how to use clapsticks, didgeridoos, boondis and make
spears. We need consistent workshops and whole days in schools around cultural
activities like making clapsticks, learning language, how to do yarning circles and
weaving. This would better connect us with community and help us to feel culturally
connected in a school setting.

There’s Aboriginal Studies at school, but there’s only Indigenous history, rather than
culture. Students could learn weaving, artworks, the stories of the 7 sisters, artefacts and
other things. The First Nations students could come up with murals and explain it to the
non-First Nations students to help them understand cultural connection, and why it’s
needed, why it’s important to keep First Nations students spiritually connected when
they are away from their community.

Young First Nations people definitely need a voice on these issues.

A lot of kids don’t have a voice. I’m a young leader back home, and here I’m also doing
this.

Kids need to stop being shut down. I don’t get why young people are ignored and
neglected all the time. Young people can give a lot of valuable insights, and can help
other people understand how young people work. Our voice is very valuable and very
much needed.

There’s also solutions in coming together. Since I came to Sydney to go to school, and
became independent, I’ve become more confident and had to stand up for myself more.
With some young people from Mt Druitt, I’m helping with creating an Aboriginal Youth
Peak for NSW. In that space, I can just be me, I can be comfortable and talk up. It’s useful
to come together with other young Aboriginal people.




                                             9
There should be other groups like this, where we all learn together as a community by
talking about what each of us have learned - where there’s no conflict and everyone can
be equally understood. We need to create spaces for us to come together in this way, for
culture and safety.

And we also need more safe spaces. A community group where we can talk or write about
racism would be good, and in the corner there’s a box where you can write down how it’s
affected you and put what you write in the box - keep it private. People have different
ways of experiencing racism and this is one way to respond to this.

There are lots of supports out there, but people don’t know about them. If I got a really,
really bad experience of racism, let’s say there was a youth program, I might not feel
comfortable talking about this experience. Maybe I might prefer to put it into a song, a
poem or rhymes, a journal. I’ve experienced racism. I don’t want my kids or their kids to
experience it growing up. Someone might set up a program that people will trust that can
make it safer for First Nations people to grow up.

We need accountability and more education. At school, one student was suspended
after a racist incident against a First Nations student who was affected emotionally, who
didn’t feel safe. Part of me thinks that’s good - they then understand that racism isn’t the
right thing. But sending them back to their family, they’re probably not going to be pulled
up at home.

While they’re suspended I think they should be required to learn about cultural and
spiritual connection, how racism impacts First Nations people - to write an essay about
these things, about why racism shouldn’t exist, why it’s bad. Then they can think about
how to apologise when the First Nations student feels safe enough to hear this. The
school needs to play a role in this, but it would be helpful to have a community member
come in and help navigate.

Police can be corrupt if they arrest someone who is Indigenous or has a cultural
background. Police can be racist too. Just because they’re part of the law doesn't mean
they’re not racist. Someone can be arrested but not know their rights. Police can hurt that
person physically, and treat them badly. Give them a bad experience. Because that
person doesn’t understand the law they wouldn’t know what actions to take to stop that
corrupt cop.

There’s a lot of racism in the justice system. Not everyone is up for taking action on it. We
need a support system for those treated badly by police - where they can learn what their
rights are and how to uphold them. Maybe a community support program where young
people can access legal information and advice before they are likely to get targeted by
police. Things that they can do to support themselves, how to speak, so they won’t be
clueless and all alone when they are in the justice system.



                                             10
Where do you get your strength from?
I draw my strength from my Elders, my ancestors, especially my dad. He is very strong
minded. We used to do marches across the bridge to have our voice heard. When I was
11, I designed the logo for the Indigenous Party of Australia. We put together the party
because of the issues, because we were being ignored, so we decided to have a voice in
parliament. I learnt my strength from my dad, because he taught me the rights and
wrongs, same as his father did. Same as his nan. They taught me what’s respectful and
what’s not, and as you get older you keep learning.

I had a lot of messages around being ‘staunch’ growing up. I still get those messages.

I cried when I got accepted into school in Sydney as I didn’t want to leave home, leave my
community and make new friends. My dad and brother brought me here. ‘Keep your head
down and focus, don’t look back, you can make changes a lot of kids in Wilcannia don’t
have the chance to do.’

I struggled with the culture shock when I got here. I was really culturally connected back
home but was new to town and there was less culture all around me. Then I started doing
cultural dancing, which helped me a lot. That’s why I think that there should be more that
schools do to help young people with culture shock, to stay connected and not be
overwhelmed by not being around community and culture anymore. It hits them hard.

When I graduated from school, my Uncle said ‘We’re proud of you, you have to keep
going.’ When I graduated, they all congratulated me, but my father had a talk with me.
‘You’ve made us proud. You can’t come back home, you have to stay down there and
make a change.’

I do want to make a change. In a workspace or school area or in any social interactions, I
want for people to look at another person and think they are just another person, I don’t
need to say anything about their cultural background. And that people don’t offend each
other, where they see each other as equals.




                                           11
1. Introduction

1.1     About the Call It Out Register

The Jumbunna Institute for Education and Research (Jumbunna Research), in
collaboration with the National Justice Project (NJP), developed Call It Out as an online
register (the Register) to record all forms and levels of racism and discrimination
experienced by First Nations peoples.1 Call It Out was officially launched on 21 March
2022 to coincide with the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

Call It Out provides a simple and secure online reporting mechanism without the usual
barriers which often inhibit reports of racism. It is intended to provide First Nations
peoples who have experienced racism in all forms and witnesses to such racism with an
accessible platform on which to share their experiences.

The Register is an independent, Indigenous-controlled reporting mechanism which is
distinct from traditional complaints and legal processes. Reports of racist issues and
incidents to complaints bodies, for instance, may be restricted or limited to specific
forms of racism, and responding to racism through antidiscrimination and other laws and
complaints mechanisms can be difficult to initiate and navigate, with often fairly
prescribed remedies available. In contrast, Call It Out is an ongoing, respondent
generated initiative with a national focus. The Register provides the opportunity to
identify patterns of racism at institutional and structural levels, including to inform
evidence-based advocacy and campaigning initiatives that proactively strive towards
eliminating racism and discrimination towards First Nations peoples in this country.

We encourage anyone who experiences or witnesses racism against Aboriginal and/or
Torres Strait Islander people to make a report using the Call It Out mobile or web app (for
more information visit callitout.com.au). You can also make a report using the print and
digital questions forms, including in Easy Read, available for download on the Call It Out
Resources page.

1.2     Aim of the Register

A key objective of Call It Out is to generate evidence to support First Nations leaders,
organisations and advocates in garnering support and resources to develop further tools



1
  We have used the terms Aboriginal, First Nations and Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander people
interchangeably. The term Indigenous is used where it is in the narrative recorded on the database. We
only use the term Indigenous when describing a ‘non-Indigenous’ person. We recognise that this
approach does not reflect the diversity of, and that there is no consensus amongst First Nations peoples
in Australia about how to be described. We apologise if this approach causes offence or
misrepresentation. This is not our intention.


                                                   12
and strategies to address racism and discrimination, including through systemic and
cultural change.

Racism and discrimination take many forms. They can be direct and indirect,
interpersonal, online and institutional, for instance. Unlike other mechanisms that are
limited by distinct parameters, Call It Out is designed to allow respondents the freedom
to share any experiences they consider relevant to shape a comprehensive
representation of First Nations peoples’ lived experiences of racism and discrimination.

By using the Register to call out racism, First Nations peoples and their allies help to tell
the true story of racism in this country. Collecting, analysing and reporting on First
Nations peoples’ experiences of racism enables us and community leaders to continue
the fight against racism and protect future generations.

Reports made to Call It Out enable Jumbunna Research together with National Justice
Project to:

    •   Develop comprehensive reports on racism and discrimination experienced by
        First Nations peoples
    •   Support First Nations organisations and leaders to identify problem areas and to
        respond to racism and discrimination
    •   Explore measures to counter racism and discrimination against First Nations
        peoples
    •   Educate the community about racism and discrimination against First Nations
        peoples
    •   Support appropriate investment in Indigenous-led anti-racism activities and
        initiatives
    •   Analyse the actions and demographics of perpetrators to better understand how
        to counter the behaviours of individuals and characteristics of systems that
        manifest as racism
    •   Measure patterns in the circumstances, nature, frequency and geographic spread
        of discrimination and racism; and
    •   Advocate for law reform and social change.

1.3     About this Report

This is the fourth report published on the information recorded in the Call It Out Register.2
This report provides analysis of the incidents of racism recorded in the Register for the


2
 Our interim first report released in 2022, providing analysis of incidents recorded on the Register during
the first six months of its operation until 20 September 2022. The second report analysed incidents
recorded over the twelve month period 21 March 2022 to 20 March 2023. A third report covered the
period 21 March 2023 to 20 March 2024. We will continue to produce Call It Out reports annually over
coming years to enable analysis of the changing nature and extent of racism over time.

                                                    13
12-month period covering 21 March 2024 to 20 March 2025. It also includes an
introduction by a young person, Amelia Whyman, a proud Malyangapa and Wankumarra
woman, speaking about issues of racism, given themes arising in this year’s report.

The Call It Out Register contains 20 questions covering the nature of the incident, details
of where and when the incident took place and who was involved, as well as possible
responses to racism. Questions ask for multiple choice and/or free text answers. To be
recorded as an incident there is a minimum threshold of recorded answers which must
be met. Questions asking for confidential information on the person completing the
report (which includes their name, email/phone number and background) and their
agreement to the use of anonymised information, along with an additional five questions
on the nature of the incident must be completed for a response to be counted as a
registration of an incident on the Register.

In March 2024, the Register was updated to better address some gaps arising from our
previous analysis and reporting. These changes are summarised below and detailed at
the relevant sections throughout this Report.

    •   Four new questions were added to record:
        o the background of the person making a report, including those by friends/family
          and witnesses (required)3
        o multiple incidents of racism (optional)
        o the age of the perpetrator (optional), and
        o barriers to standing up against racism (optional).
    •   Two previously optional questions were added to the minimum threshold of
        recorded answers: where the racism happened; and who was the perpetrator.
    •   The multiple-choice answers were revised for nine questions (both required and
        optional): how the racism was experienced or witnessed; the type of racism
        experienced or witnessed; where the racism happened; who perpetrated the racism;
        emotional responses to racism; other responses to racism; and strategies for
        combatting racism.
    •   Three optional questions were revised to limit the number of multiple-choice
        answers a respondent can select to a maximum of three answers: emotional
        responses to racism; other responses to racism; and strategies for combatting
        racism. (This limit was also applied to the new question on barriers to standing up
        against racism mentioned above.)



3
 Prior to 21 March 2024, the Register did not record the Aboriginality of third parties (witnesses, family
members or friends).


                                                     14
Over the twelve-month period 21 March 2024 to 20 March 2025, there were 458
registrations of incidents on the database which fulfilled these criteria. From the 458
registrations we removed 15 reports which were made by individuals who used the
platform to promote racism. We removed a further registration which was a valid report
of racism that targeted persons who were not Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander.
The total number of validated reports used for the analysis in this report is 442. It should
be noted that this is a count of registrations rather than incidents and a single registration
can cover ongoing or multiple events, incidents or issues, including those that are
structural, rather than occurring at a single point in time. We note that in this report we
have used the term ‘racism’ to describe it in all its forms, along with discrimination based
on race, racial vilification and racist violence.4

There are two Appendices incorporating all data tables utilised in this report. Appendix
A includes data tables from all 442 registrations. Appendix B includes data tables
relating to the section on children and young people at [4].

The quotations used in this report are drawn from the narratives shared to the Register.
Throughout this report the quotations which are identified as ‘Self-report’ are drawn
from reports entered into the Register by First Nations people who directly experienced
the racism reported. The quotations by someone reporting racism on behalf of their First
Nations friends or family are identified as ‘Friend or relative report’. All other witnesses
of racism are identified as ‘Witness report’.

Quotations are also identified by the person’s background, where they have chosen to
share this information in their report. A person’s background is identified as ‘Aboriginal’,
‘Torres Strait Islander’, ‘Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander’ or ‘non-Indigenous’.

Quotations which are identified as ‘Self-report’ are also identified by the person’s
gender, where they have chosen to share this information. A person’s gender is identified
as ‘female’, ‘male’ or ‘non-binary’. In this report, ‘witness’ and ‘friend or relative’
reports are not identified by gender as Call It Out records the gender of the person
experiencing racism, which is not always the person reporting it.

We have also removed any identifying details about victims or perpetrators from all
quotations to maintain privacy, except in some cases where these are already in the
public domain.




4
  We also note that although our focus in this report is on race-based issues, we acknowledge that
individuals may experience these issues alongside other forms of discrimination (based on disability,
age, etc.).

2.1    Who reported the incident and where they reported

Individuals completing the Register were
asked to identify whether they are
Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander
or non-Indigenous. This was a new
compulsory question for a registration to
be accepted.

As shown in Figure 1, almost half of all
respondents (199/442 or 45%) identified
as either Aboriginal (42%), Torres Strait
Islander (1%) or both Aboriginal and
Torres Strait Islander (2%). Just over half
identified as non-Indigenous (51%). The
remainder chose not to provide this
information (4%). (See also Table 1 in
Appendix A).

Individuals completing the Register were also asked to identify whether they were a ‘First
Nations person who experienced racism’, a ‘friend or relative of a First Nations person
who experienced racism’ or a ‘witness of racism towards a First Nations person’. This
was a compulsory question for a registration to be accepted.

2.2     How the incident was experienced or witnessed

Individuals completing the Register were asked how the incident was experienced or
witnessed. This was a compulsory question for a registration to be accepted.

The categories for selection were ‘interpersonal racism’, ‘systemic/institutional racism’,
‘both interpersonal and systemic/institutional racism’, and 'other’. The Register defines
‘interpersonal’ racism as 'person to person' racism. ‘Systemic/Institutional’ racism is
defined as occurring 'where system, organisation or institutional policies systematically
treat First Nations people unfairly'.

As shown in Figure 4, just over
a third of all incidents were
witnessed or experienced as
interpersonal racism (34%). A
third of incidents were
witnessed or experienced as
both      interpersonal    and
systemic/institutional racism
(33%). More than one in five
incidents were witnessed or
experienced as systemic/
institutional racism (21%).
(See also Table 4 in Appendix
A).

First Nations people reporting
direct experiences of racism
were more likely to categorise
incidents as both interpersonal and systemic/institutional, while third parties
(friends/relatives and witnesses) were more likely to identify incidents as interpersonal
racism (Table 4, Appendix A). For those who responded ‘other’, most incidents recorded
occurred within social media, or witnessed online.8 It may be that for those selecting
‘other’, these types of incidents are difficult to categorise as interpersonal,
systemic/institutional racism or both.

We note too that there is not always consistency in how individuals are categorising their
reports across these different categories, meaning that the statistics set out above need
to be interpreted alongside accounts shared as qualitative data. Categorisation can be
subjective.


8
 These reports commonly referred to skits of a particular female comedian, see below at [2.3.1]. We note
too that witnesses of racism were proportionately more likely to select ‘other’ (42/56 or 75%) than those
who self-reported (14/56 or 25%) (Table 4, Appendix A).

                                                   18
As an example, racist incidents identified as ‘interpersonal’ were sometimes but not
always also categorised as ‘systemic/institutional’ where racism perpetrated by an
individual was clearly connected with broader historical, cultural and other contexts or
systems. For example, this was the approach taken by one witness reporting an incident
involving a Church Dean who had replaced the Aboriginal flag outside his cathedral with
the church’s ensign.

       The decision to remove the Aboriginal flag was challenged by an older lady who
       has been very involved in justice activism for many years, to which the Dean
       responded by shutting the conversation down. What stands out to me is the
       dynamic of contempt and erasure of present-day understandings of the questions
       being broached. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

The report goes on to set out in full a message from the Church Dean, published with a
print of the 1908 Commonwealth coat of arms and interpreted by the witness as being
dismissive of negative perceptions of Australia Day celebrations (arising because of the
day’s association with colonisation, discussed in our last annual report). The Dean
wrote, ‘It is sad though that some strident voices seem to want to erase the presence and
legitimacy of people other than Indigenous people in this land.’ The witness places this
incident in wider context and also notes that raising the issue with the Bishop (as a
representative of the Church more senior than the Dean) would be pointless. ‘The person
least likely to be receptive to feedback is the bishop. This fellow is his man.’

       Since this message was published a number of parishioners have remarked that
       the atmosphere of the cathedral has become much more adversarial. There are
       broader psycho-social safety dynamics to this situation that make it an inherently
       unsafe place for Aboriginal people. In a church that has prided itself on being open
       to everyone without judgement, this represents a major degradation of the
       culture. On the next [Call It Out Register] question I'm ticking ‘multiple incidents’
       because this is something that is wider than a ‘single incident’. This is an instance
       of a culture shift that allows bigger forms of race-based contempt to be displayed.
       (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

As a further example of the way in which different forms of racism interact, an incident
occurring in a university setting was also identified as both interpersonal (racism
perpetrated by an individual student) and systemic (where the institution responded
poorly).

       Interpersonal racism came from university student against me … verbally in class
       with an audience, privately via emails, and via the media … Institutional racism
       came from university 'support' services, university executive and university legal
       team in the way they handled my reporting of the student's behaviour in class and
       via work email. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)


                                            19
And finally, we received multiple reports about a mainstream media interview in which
the non-Indigenous interviewer raised (completely irrelevant) past actions of a young
First Nations man being interviewed about his win in a fishing competition. 9

       A young Aboriginal man was publicly humiliated and shamed by a well-known
       Caucasian television journalist in an 'interview' about catching a prize-winning
       barramundi. The presenter/journalist used the interview as an opportunity to
       discriminate against the young man, raising the issue of criminal behaviour in the
       young man's past which had absolutely nothing to do with catching the
       barramundi, thereby vilifying the young man and reinforcing negative stereotypes
       about Aboriginal people. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

As the report states, the actions of a single journalist, in this case, tipped over into
systemic racism as the media company in question saw no issue with the question being
asked and the interview being broadcast.

       It is completely unacceptable journalism and representative of the systemic
       racism within the news organisation that this was allowed to occur and air on
       national television. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

2.3.1 Racist stereotyping

Racist attitudes or stereotyping is the predominant type of racism identified in the
Register (30%). The pervasive nature of stereotyping is also indicated by the extent to
which it is identified as ‘ongoing’ by those using the Register (25%) (see Table 12 in
Appendix A and [2.5] below). As highlighted in our earlier reporting, racist attitudes and
stereotyping underpin racism in most or all contexts in which it arises.

We saw the same types of stereotyping/racist attitudes reported this year as in previous
years. Common examples describe First Nations people as law breakers or as otherwise
engaging in anti-social or negative behaviour, misusing alcohol/drugs, seeking or
receiving financial benefits or ‘hand-outs’ they don’t deserve (and related to this, also
avoiding taxes or employment) and not looking or acting ‘Black’ enough to be Indigenous.

The following reports detail instances of stereotyping. Note the reference in the first
report below to the term ‘natives’, relevant to discussion below of links between present-
day and historical racism.

         I was travelling from [named town in NSW] airport to a hotel for a work conference
         and was talking to the driver. The conversation started out fine. We discussed the

2.3.2 Aggressive racism

Verbal abuse/hate speech was the second most common type of racism disclosed
(17%). This and other forms of what we have termed ‘aggressive racism’ are evidenced in
many reports, however. We identify bullying, threats, intimidation (12%), physical harm
(3%) and damage to property (1%) as ‘aggressive racism’. Taken together, these types of
aggressive racism comprised a relatively high 33% of all responses (see Figure 5 above,
and Table 5 in Appendix A). Aggressive racism also constituted 35% of all incidents
reported as ongoing (see Table 12 in Appendix A and below at [2.5]).

Reports of verbal abuse and hate speech may link to other forms of racism, including
stereotyping (for example, related to criminality of First Nations people). Incidents may
be private (for example, in family conversations) and/or public in nature.

       Someone put [up] a video of people in their yard trespassing and a guy
       commented "uncivilised koons (sic) at it again". (Witness report, Aboriginal)

       I tried to talk to my father about why Australia day (Invasion day) is harmful to the
       First Nations peoples and he called me a "<n word> lover." (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

Reports describing more public incidents described use
of hate speech or symbols in the workplace and online
social media posts, including comments referencing the
Klu Klux Klan (KKK) or lynching of First Nations people, for
instance.

                           The guy [shared social media profile] promotes lynching of
                           First Nations people. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

                           meeting', which made the rest of the staff that were present

                           stumbled on a property with Nazi symbols. I have researched
                           online and found this place and the Nazi symbols have been

       everyone to hear. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       [An Aboriginal man] was undertaking his tertiary course and bullied for his
       wardrobe but then escalated into threats of violence due to his Aboriginal
       background. A man came up to him with a deodorant can and lighter in class and
       asked [this man] if he wanted to "get burnt". (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

A witness reported multiple posts by an individual on
Facebook, one of which called for the restoration of past
policy ‘permitting’ the shooting of Aboriginal people
(witness report, non-Indigenous).

Online incidents were sometimes reported as provoking
and encouraging real-life incidents of violence - and First
Nations young people are a common target in this context
(see further below [4.3]).

       Aboriginal family in a home targeted by white
       person because of racism and hate. The white man
       targeted the home and went to "confront" the family and then returned setting the
       house alight with a Molotov cocktail. The man has since been charged by [police]
       but the build-up to the incident included online hate and community members of
       the Facebook group encouraging the racialised violence. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

Incidents involving harassment and intimidation included the mainstream media
interview conducted with a First Nations young person who won a fishing competition,
referred to in [2.2].

       [Named journalist] harassed and intimidated a young Black man on public
       television. Blatantly racist attitude and stereotyping. This is racist and it's
       defamation. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Online incidents also included targeted intimidation and harassment of First Nations
individuals, including those seen as ‘activist’ or as having an opinion (for example, if
commenting on racist content).

       It has come to my attention my [Facebook] profile is being shared onto racists’
       pages. These people also send me messages, saying "they don't like Aboriginal
       activists.” Sharing my profile pic again and again. [This particular person is] online
       speaking of creating an army and he has people who follow him and participate in
       the harassment and my profile shares. Go to these peoples’ pages and you will
       see the extremism of this. I have not spoken to these people. They are sharing a



                                            26
        profile pic of mine from the Referendum last year. I perform in a band for a living,
        I'm a little worried I'm being targeted. (Self-report, Aboriginal)

        After engaging in a public commentary on Facebook, a user decided [to] message
        me directly to carry on with their views regarding the superiority of white
        Australians and compare with First Nations peoples in a direct attempt to assert
        superiority. The same user has now decided to post passive derogatory
        comments about [First Nations peoples] on my personal page which is public.
        (Self-report, not identified)

Again, harassment and intimidation also occurred in-person or as ‘real-life’ incidents,
including as follows.

        Non Aboriginal neighbour of Aunt is racially abusing her and forcing her to leave
        her public housing unit where she was so happy and safe. (Friend/Relative report,
        non-Indigenous)

        We had just finished watching State of Origin and a white male was coming home
        across the street - this time he gave us the finger, the second time he came onto
        my property and threw an egg at the window, the third time he came around and
        moved the mirrors on the car. Believe this was racially motivated as an act of
        racial hate against Aboriginals. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

2.3.3 Laws, policies, practice

Systemic or institutional racism has again been reported with relative frequency to Call
It Out. As discussed earlier, when describing how the incident was experienced or
witnessed, reports of systemic/institutional racism on its own constituted 21% of all
reports, while experiences of both interpersonal and systemic/institutional were
identified in 33% of all reports.14 Thus, taken together, 54% of people described
experiencing the incident as systemic/institutional racism.

As noted above, the Register defines ‘systemic/institutional’ racism as occurring 'where
system, organisation or institutional policies systematically treat First Nations people
unfairly'. Related to this, this year we included ‘law, policies and practices that lead to
unfair treatment and negative outcomes’ as one category of ‘type of racism’. Just over
one in ten (12%) of all reports were identified as falling into this category (Figure 5 above).
In the discussion below we draw some links between this type of racism and
systemic/institutional racism, as reported to the Register.




14
  See above at [2.2] and Figure 4, and Table 4 in Appendix A. See also the discussion of location and
perpetrator of incidents below at [2.3], [2.4], [2.5.3] and [2.6], and of racism specifically related to the
criminal legal system below at [2.4.4].

                                                      27
As a starting point, failure to adequately provide for First Nations-led decision-making at
both a policy and legislative level on issues impacting First Nations people was raised as
an issue of broad relevance.

       Government institutions know what the F they need to do! They even say they are
       going to do it or already are. But they are appalling in their omission-to pass
       control and decision making back to First Nations people – in justice, health
       education and really – everywhere. Why is this so hard!!? (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

More specifically, one report spoke of legislation impacting decision-making of First
Nations people in the NT. This report relates to the Territory Coordinator Bill, which
bestowed substantive powers on a government appointed ‘Territory Coordinator’. The
bill is identified as permitting the NT Government ‘to override dozens of laws relevant to
projects of "economic significance”’. It passed into law in 2025, ‘despite strong
opposition from leading Indigenous groups and legal experts’ (witness report, non-
Indigenous). Aboriginal Land Councils in the NT identified the bill as excluding ‘Aboriginal
people from involvement in development decisions on their traditional lands’ and
preventing them from ‘protecting their land and culture’.15 The Territory Coordinator, for
instance, is granted powers to declare a Territory Development or Infrastructure
Coordination Area on Aboriginal land and Native Title areas without consent or
consultation with Traditional Owners, as examples.16

Laws, policies and practices that appear neutral (do not single out First Nations people
for negative treatment intentionally or at all) may have disproportionately negative
impacts on this group in their application. Criminal laws which may not explicitly target
but have reasonably foreseeable negative impacts on First Nations people were called
out in this context, including Victorian bail laws.17

       The Bail Amendment (Stage One) Act (Vic) 2017 and Bail Amendment (Stage Two)
       Act (Vic) 2018 saw changes to the Bail Act (Vic) 1977. There amendments had a
       discriminatory effect on First Nations People - especially those in incarceration
       awaiting trial or a hearing. While the Bail Amendment Act (Vic) 2023
       addressed/repealed some of these discriminatory amendments, there is still a
       discriminatory foundation to the Bail Act (Vic) 1977 that needs to be addressed so
       as to make the Act more equitable for all communities. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

                                               28
Related to this, also described was the way in which different institutions or systems
come together to discriminate against First Nations people. This occurs, for instance,
where criminal legislation or policy (again, in this instance, Victorian bail laws) are
introduced by government in part as a reaction to perceived threats to law and order so
often a focus for the media. This year we once again received reports of the deliberate
targeting of First Nations people in media reporting.

       Knee-jerk and racist bail reforms announced by Victoria last week, including
       removal of the principle of detention as a last resort for children and young
       people. … Plus, the accompanying fear mongering by certain media outlets, e.g.
       [named media outlet] ran 21 stories and launched a petition pushing for reforms
       in the week before the reforms were unveiled by [named non-Indigenous female
       politician in Victoria]. Examples of titles include crap like “Suburbs under siege”,
       “Taking back our streets”. Sorry but whose land is it, White mate? (Witness report,
       non-Indigenous)

Zoning laws that prohibited public drinking were identified as more likely to negatively
impact Aboriginal people (and as being intended to do so). Police discretion in
implementing these and other laws (for example, move-on laws) were also reported –
with police-based racial profiling of First Nations young people singled out in some
instances (see [4.3]).

       Drinking laws in the NT … exclude areas such as [named town, NT] and [named
       town, NT] where white people drink [and] … discriminate solely against Aboriginal
       people drinking in public. (Friend/Relative report, non-Indigenous)

       Increased police numbers and increased powers to keep First Nations away from
       CBD. Law and Order response to social problems. Strongly supported by the
       general population. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

As this last report indicates, racism within government systems can be linked to
community-embedded racist attitudes. These attitudes create the conditions in which
the justice system perpetrates racism.

       Society is the perpetrator – the justice system is the mechanism through which
       we continue to colonise and keep Aboriginal people in their place.
       (Friend/Relative report, non-Indigenous)

In terms of neutral but discriminatory policy, the following incident relates to First
Nations’ access to services that fail to meet their needs.

       As the majority of people I look after are Aboriginal, I regularly see and hear of local
       businesses and attitudes negatively treat[ing] the locals [sic]. There is so much
       red tape that gets in the way of assisting my [clients] as the standards of servicing
       DO NOT CATER for common local Aboriginal circumstances such as: Lack of


                                             29
        community or personal transport, No ID, No Phone, homelessness, Drug and
        Alcohol etc... (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Education-related policy in the NT was also reported; specifically, that schools record
Aboriginal student absences in ways that fail to account for cultural reasons for non-
attendance. The negative consequences of this for Aboriginal education are also
highlighted (that is, reduced funding).18

        Students attending NT Dept Ed Schools are classed as having 'unacceptable
        absence' for periods of time spent at an outstation, being cultural homelands
        located far from the school they're enrolled at. Outstations provide important
        connections to country, to family, to lore, to ceremony, to language, to all things
        that embody identity. When students are classed as having 'unacceptable
        attendance' the student is then removed from the census of the school. Census
        data informs funding for each school. So remote schools suffer when students
        are unable to 'attend' their enrolled setting due to travel to outstations and their
        parents don't provide 'acceptable' reasons for the students absence. (Witness
        report, non-Indigenous)

As discussed earlier, interpersonal racism may interconnect with institutional racism.
This includes where is is perpetrated by individuals as a pattern of behaviour. The
following examples report such a pattern, in this case involving multiple staff
perpetrating racism within health services. The incidents impact First Nations patients
and their families, staff and the local First Nations community.

        Bullying and harassment of Aboriginal staff. Poor treatment of patients in
        Aboriginal health service. Turning patients away from service, speaking down to
        and dismissing Aboriginal patients. Treating local people badly. (Witness report,
        non-Indigenous)

        Aboriginal man dying of renal failure was treated in an appalling way at a major
        western Sydney hospital. He was left in the hallway, ignored and when he did get
        a room after a few days he was not cleaned or given appropriate food. I observed

       very negative comments about him from staff. The family was very distressed and
       no one cared. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

The behaviour of individuals, whether or not it occurs as a pattern, may also constitute
institutional racism where incidents go unchecked or are otherwise poorly addressed
(including preventatively). There are multiple reports to Call It Out describing institutional
failure to avoid or eliminate racism impacting First Nations people (see also [3.3], [3.4]).
Linking in with the category of racism ‘law, policy or practice’, appropriate procedures
and policies that might check racist ‘practice’ on the part of individuals may be absent
or just poorly implemented, as the following education related example suggests.

       Institution not adhering to their own policies. Choosing to treat an Aboriginal
       student by not following specific wording in their own policies and disadvantaging
       the student unfairly. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Other reports referred to tokenistic efforts of organisations to set up Reconciliation
Action Plans (RAPs), cultural safety frameworks or similar. Health was again highlighted
in this respect.

       There are too many incidences and experiences of racism to list. Health
       organisation health equity strategy / framework does not align with what is
       required to address or eliminate racial discrimination and institutional racism.
       The proposed strategies are influenced by Western ideologies, systems and
       structures. Health organisations lack understanding and respect on community
       engagement and consultation. (Self-report, Aboriginal)

Some reported RAPs or similar policy being developed without any real substance and in
some cases, apparently in order to derive a commercial or financial benefit. The
following incident identifies this as occurring in a corporate mining context.

       The discriminatory practices within [named company] extend beyond individual
       interactions to systemic issues such as the misuse of the Reconciliation Action
       Plan (RAP). It is deeply concerning to learn that the company may have entered
       into RAP agreements solely for the purpose of securing business, rather than
       genuinely committing to reconciliation and addressing issues of Indigenous
       inequality. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

‘Black cladding’ was also called out - arising where a largely non-Indigenous controlled
organisation presents itself to be Indigenous controlled or led in order to win tenders or
otherwise derive benefit.

       Our business [named company] (100% Indigenous owned) was exploited and
       defrauded by [named charity] and [named not for profit]. We were in a consortium
       led by [named charity] that won a $5m federal government grant. We were
       excluded from consultations, denied transparency or viewing the grant


                                             31
       application and denied appropriate funding. When the grant was won, we were
       pressured to step down from the consortium, placed on a 12month contract,
       denied reasonable funding, forced into involuntary servitude and paid $23,000 for
       14 months of work, co-design, content design and workshop planning,
       development, marketing and delivery. When we complained about the injustice
       of being severely financially discriminated against, our contract was terminated
       because of "lacking capacity to deliver the five year program we co-designed" …
       The entire process was co-designed by white women charity leaders to
       significantly disadvantage the only Indigenous business in the consortium … This
       process indicates how charity leaders intentionally co-design disadvantage in
       federal government grants to benefit their organisations and cause profound
       financial detriment to Indigenous businesses. (Self-report, Torres Strait Islander
       female)

As a related incident of racism, a councillor was reported as publicly questioning
payment to First Nations people for their expertise in guiding local government policy.

       A councillor on [named town] Council made derogatory commentary about the
       procurement of Aboriginal people to consult and engage [named town] City
       Council and Aboriginal people in developing a commitment and action plan for
       the council. The councillor named the advisors, criticised their integrity,
       publicised the fee, questioned the value of the service, criticised the cultural
       safety training and expertise of the cultural safety practitioner. The post was put
       on Facebook and people commented with racist, uninformed, derogatory
       comments. This councillor of [named town] incited that racism. (Friend/Relative
       report, non-Indigenous)

As some of the above examples indicate, laws, policies and practices developed or
implemented within government systems and institutions may be identified as
institutionally racist. We discuss below in detail at [2.4.4] reports about the criminal legal
system, as a specific example of this. The child protection system was also called out.
Incidents were raised about its systemic failure to work culturally and otherwise
appropriately with First Nations families and communities. This includes failure to
adhere to government policy designed to protect the rights of Aboriginal people
interacting with this system (note the overlap with non-recognition of cultural rights,
discussed below at [2.3.4]).

       [Named government agency/service] treated a family in a racist manner by not
       recognising that mob is important in Aboriginal families. Young mother was
       targeted to have non Aboriginal respite care while [named government
       agency/service] ignored the many female family members who wanted to assist
       her. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)



                                             32
       [Named government agency/service] worker did not allow Aboriginal parent to
       express their views. Allowed a non-Aboriginal support person (asked for by the
       Aboriginal parent) to be told that 'we are not interested in your white views'. Used
       threatening language to suggest their child would not ever be returned. Shamed
       the parent by reminding them they were the 'problem'. Did not follow the
       [Aboriginal case management policy]. Allowed Aboriginal workers to support the
       humiliation. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

       Child removed from Aboriginal parent under ROSH (Risk of Significant Harm).
       Aboriginal grandmother and great grandmother were refused their care.
       Child went to non-Aboriginal non-related person and remains there after 18
       months despite grandmother being a very suitable person to care for them.
       Report made on grandmother contained false and racist comments. Report was
       compiled by agency employed by [named government agency/service]. (Witness
       report, non-Indigenous)

The above reports and the one that follows point to poor accountability within the child
protection system for non-compliance with policy, including for NGOs funded to support
Aboriginal families interacting with this system.

The above incidents describe limited accountability on the part of government. The
following report identifies that NGOs funded to support Aboriginal families interacting
with this system are similarly not held accountable for failure to comply with relevant
policy.

       An NGO organisation worker allowed the OOHC carer to be abusive to the
       Aboriginal family by telling them that the children belonged to her not them. She
       was given their address so then intervened on monthly visits causing distress and
       humiliation. Aboriginal family rights/complaints were ignored. Cultural practices
       of the family were trivialised. Family now do not see their children … I am
       saddened and shocked by the [Aboriginal case management policy] being ignored
       and the ferocity of the racist attitude towards the family. The NGO receives over
       $5,000,000 of govt funding. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Finally, racism can be seen as political in nature and as situated within our political
system. A number of reports referred to incidents that they felt reflected racism as ‘right-
wing’, for instance (including when referring to the racist skit of the comedian discussed
above) or as emanating from politicians and media personalities who are ‘far-right
populist and conservative’ commentating on ‘identitity politics’ (witness report, non-
Indigenous).19

2.3.4 Cultural and other Indigenous rights

Those using the Call It Out Register have the option to select ‘Didn't recognise cultural
rights/protocols (e.g. Kinship, Sorry Business, Acknowledgement of Country)’ to
describe the incident reported. Multiple reports did so (11% of all reports, see Figure 5
above and Table 5 in Appendix A). As was the case in previous years, reports described
non-recognition of Indigenous sovereign, cultural and spiritual connections to land and
country.

       Multiple comments [online] on marine park and First Nations people having
       special privileges with Cultural fishing practices. Non- Aboriginal people feel like
       it's reverse racism and we have special privileges. (Self-report, Aboriginal)

       A non-Indigenous relative (half-sister with a non-Indigenous father) and I got into
       a discussion about Uluru and how people used to be able to walk up the rock. She
       said she would walk it if she could. I said that's disrespectful to our Indigenous
       Australians who had asked that people do not walk on the rock. She said, 'nobody
       owns a rock'. Then we got into an argument about the politics. She said that I don't
       understand and it's a complex matter. I tried to tell her she doesn't understand my
       connection to country and spirit/ancestors and it's about respecting that … She
       also said 'she didn't cause what had happened' and 'every country gets invaded'.
       (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Reports called out local government Councillors and once again, health staff.

       During NAIDOC march down main street of [named town, NSW], [a] Shire Council
       Chamber employee stated, "What a waste of time". This is an Aboriginal
       community. The Shire Council Chambers have predominately white staff and
       have regularly displayed disdain and ignorance of the local Aboriginal residents of
       the Shire. Staff were not even aware of the NAIDOC march taking place today even
       though they are responsible for the road closures. There was no signage up
       informing of the local event or decoration celebrating NAIDOC week. Disgusting
       display today from staff. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

       I work for a small country hospital. We had an Aboriginal gentleman transferred
       from a larger hospital to our site. He had advanced cancer and was under the
       palliative pathway. His wish was to "die on country" hence he was transferred to
       our hospital. During shift handover shortly after the patient arrived I was
       explaining why the patient had transferred to our hospital. One of my coworkers
       responded "to die on country? … So, what... We have to lay him on the ground?"
       Then proceeded to start laughing. My colleagues intercepted and explained the
       concept of "on country" and she replied that she understood what it meant but
       just thought that it was "silly". My colleagues also mocked his family members.
       This patient had some family members who were incarcerated and sought


                                            34
      permission for compassionate leave from the prison to visit the patient. Some
      staff commented that they should've thought about their actions more and other
      derogatory comments regarding Aboriginal people within the justice system.
      (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Dismissal of and push back against an Acknowledgement of/Welcome to Country were
reported, as was the case in previous Call It Out reporting.

      I'm a local government worker who responds to an event feedback form on my
      section of our website. I got a submission … from someone complaining about an
      event they attended … The submission content read: "What a fantastic evening,
      sadly spoilt by the fact that we had to sit through a lecture from an Indigenous
      person who put themselves above everyone else, my views were shared by almost
      all within my seating area! I didn't drive 3.5 hrs & spend $400 on tickets to listen to
      her misplaced BS! No recognition of my father & grandfather, my mates who
      fought for our land, sorry but the welcome to country went out the door at the
      Voice referendum and you should do the same." (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

      Someone on my local Facebook page wrote "Can you imagine, you're an Aussie.
      You was born and lived and worked your entire life in Australia and you are now in
      your 80s. And you have to listen to a 19 year old girl tell you to make
      acknowledgement of country ... what a load of crap." And comments followed
      being completely ignorant about the history of Australia. (Self-report, Aboriginal
      female)

As noted below in [2.4], education was one of the more commonly identified locations
where racism occurs. We set out education related incidents throughout this report, one
of which is as follows.

      I have been working with [this student] for the past semester on a project about
      Indigenous literacy in remote Australia. Throughout this subject he has been
      awfully racist, taking any chance to undermine the struggles of First Nations
      people and promote a colonial mindset. When I said we need an
      acknowledgement of country before our presentation, he said "we don't need that
      *face palm emoji*". When I made a comment he didn't fully agree with he (a white
      boy) sent a black thumbs-down emoji. Unprompted he went on a rant about how
      voting Yes in last year's referendum would mean [named beach, NSW] would lose
      a car park (wtf?? like okay????). Finally, when I asked what custodial lands does
      he live on (in reference to writing an acknowledgment of country for the beginning
      of our report) he said "as far as I'm concerned, I live in [(colonially) named town,
      NSW] on the land of the [(colonially) named town, NSW] people". (Witness report,
      non-Indigenous)

where the incident reported

question, answered by all the

  See: <https://nit.com.au/10-09-2025/20181/victorian-police-admit-being-caught-off-guard-by-camp-

There was an increase of five percentage points in reports of incidents occurring in a
school/educational setting compared with 2023-24. Related to this was an increase in
reports of racism against children and young people aged 10-19 years (see below at
[2.7.2]). We discuss school-based incidents in a stand-alone section focused on
children and young people at [4.2]. Incidents related to other educational settings
(including TAFE, university) are discussed throughout the report (for example, as

As another notable difference in the data, in 2024-25 there was a decrease in reports of
racism occurring in a public setting (down 6 percentage points from last year), perhaps
reflecting that in our 2023-24 reporting we recorded a spike in public incidents of racism
occurring during the 2023 Referendum period.

There was some variation in locations identified by different groups reporting to the
Register, as follows (see Table 6, Appendix A).

     ● For First Nations people reporting experiences of racism, the more common
       location of incidents was the workplace (15%), followed by social media (13%)
       and educational settings (12%).
     ● For friends/relatives, the more common location identified was educational
       settings (22%) (10-15 percentage points higher compared with other groups). This
       group also more frequently reported racism in a private setting (by 7-8 percentage
       points, compared with other groups).

2.4.1 Racism online and in the media

Overall, social media/online racism (22%) in combination with other media (7%)
constituted nearly one in three of all locations identified (29%). There were differences
across groups, however – with witnesses, for instance, proportionately more frequently
identifying these as the location of racism reported (43%)22 (see Table 6 in Appendix A).

Similar to last year, many online/media incidents demonstrated racist attitudes,
including about the so-called ‘criminality’ of First Nations people.

        Member of various local Facebook groups where individuals constantly post
        racist remarks about [First Nations’ people] perpetuating crime within the area, I
        always report to have them removed. One example was when [a] stolen car
        crashed killing 4 of the teenage FN (First Nations) occupants. The comments
        online were absolutely disgusting. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

The media interview that raised the past criminal history of the young fishing competition
winner is also relevant in this context (see [2.2]). This interview was identified as both
