drawing on and perpetuating negative stereotypes about criminality. As a further report
identifies, media reporting based on this same stereotype feeds into racist content
online.

       Biased reports on mainstream media about violence in the Northern Territory TV
       news services … systematically and overtly report on Aboriginal people
       perpetrating violence. There is never any coverage of the inflicted pain and trauma
       from predominantly white, affluent Australians towards Aboriginal people in the
       community. Immediately after these news reports, I often witness a dramatic
       increase in racially based venomous language generally directed towards
       Aboriginal people. Comments include statements to the effect that "they are just
       black bastards" or "they should all be locked up". These are indiscriminate
       comments and are not based on any idea of justice but focus on the idea of
       inflicting punishment upon the whole community in a violent way. This occurs
       every time such a news broadcast occurs without referencing the repression
       already imposed on Aboriginal people from institutions and businesses
       throughout Australia. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

It is worth pointing out too that we again received reports identifying social media/the
media as spaces in which racism may be ‘made visible’ or called out. These reports
describe published media articles that deal with racist incidents/issues or people
challenging racism on social media, for example. One relevant report concerns a TikTok
video made by a First Nations person calling out the above fishing competition interview.
This report identifies that members of the public are posting racist comments in
response to the TikTok video and that other members of the public are calling out the
interview, alongside the TikTok video creator.

       There's a bunch of racist commenters on an Indigenous person's video regarding
       the interaction between the new Indigenous teenager millionaire and the [named]
       interviewer. This particular racist commenter kept on saying that Indigenous
       people are criminals and using racial slurs. They were basically harassing them
       and they won't back down. I'm about to report them as I write this. I hope TikTok
       holds them accountable and removes their content and account. (Witness report,
       Aboriginal)

All other types of racism discussed in [2.3] are evident in online/media related reports,
including hate speech/verbal abuse, bullying, harassment and other forms of aggressive
racism (see [2.3.2]).

       [Named social media account] runs a page that systematically attacks and
       racially abuses anyone or anything associated with mob. He is a proud ex-military
       veteran. And has images of [Indigenous] inmates directly taken from inside
       [prison] ... he shames them publicly, names, family details, crimes with images of
       them inside unit blocks … His abuse is tormenting and has a group of other racist

                                           39
       minions also systematically abusing anyone in comments sections of Indigenous
       promoting sites. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

       The [named Aboriginal TV/Radio journalist/presenter] was subjected to racist
       posts on Instagram and X today. With people taunting him using fake Aboriginal
       sentence construction and others saying pass the goon boss and other offensive
       and racist remarks. Instagram and X did not moderate these offensive comments.
       (Self-report, non-identified male)

As a further example, the following report relates to a Facebook post about claims to
native title and as such, potentially also constitutes non-recognition of cultural and
Indigenous rights.

       There is a publican that owns [named pub/hotel, QLD]. He has just said to get
       ready for a race war. He is inciting people to join and fight against Indigenous
       people … The whole comment section is vile! People are threatening to cull us
       Indigenous people. (Self-report, Aboriginal, female)

2.4.2 Racism in public spaces, commercial places and transport

Racism was identified as occurring in a public setting in 7% of reports and in a
commercial setting in 8% of reports. Public transport was identified as the location for
racism in 4% of reports (see Figure 6 above and Table 6 in Appendix A).

We note the cross-over in incidents occurring in these three locations with certain forms
of racism.

   •   Shunning or excluding was identified in 7% of all reports. While less frequently
       reported overall, this type of racism was relatively frequently identified as the type
       of racism occurring in commercial locations (14%) and on public transport (15%).
   •   The combined incidents of aggressive racism (verbal abuse, bullying, threats,
       intimidation, physical harm and damage to property) accounted for 42% of all
       public setting incidents reported, 32% of all commercial places incidents
       reported and 45% of all public transport incident reported. (See Table 7 in
       Appendix A).

This cross-over is evident in the reports shared on the Register. For example, reports
identified transport operators as refusing to carry Indigenous passengers.

       I am from Whadjuk Country and couldn't even get a taxi in my own Country. (Self-
       report, Aboriginal female)

       Bus driver failed to pick up 3 Aboriginal passengers in the CBD who were waiting
       at bus stop and had waved for bus to stop. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)




                                            40
       The bus driver stopped the bus … and asked the four passengers to get off the bus.
       After they told the driver that they needed to travel further along the route, the
       driver called over two security guards who were at the transfer station, who then
       got on the bus and started interrogating the four passengers about 'what was
       going on, why won't you get off, and where are you going'. The security guards were
       being extremely abusive and intimidating. The driver then drove off towards the
       city with the security guards still on board. Two or three stops along … the driver
       pulled over and told the four passengers to get off the bus. The passengers left the
       bus, along with one of the security guards. The other security guard got off the bus
       at one or two more stops along [named street]. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Other passengers can also shun or exclude First Nations people.

       Myself and my daughter in law’s mother [named individual, Aboriginal] (my
       grandchildren's maternal grandmother) were waiting for the train in [named town,
       WA] Underground after going to the Royal Show. We were loaded up with show
       bags and gifts for our grandchildren and [my daughter in law’s mother] needed to
       sit and rest, and there was a spare seat next to a white woman available near us.
       [She] walked over to sit down and the woman began blocking the seat and trying
       to force her teenaged son standing nearby to sit in the seat and prevented [her]
       from sitting there. It was obvious the woman was intentionally blocking her, the
       gestures she was making were exaggerated and dramatic. We tried to be polite
       and acknowledged she might have legitimately wanted her son to have a seat so
       just politely nodded and (moved/walked) away. A few minutes later a white man
       came and sat in the [same] seat … and she didn't even lift her head or try and
       prevent him sitting. She made it openly clear that it was just our Aboriginality that
       was the issue. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

As reports above and those that follow indicate, First Nations people travelling on public
transport are subjected to over-surveillance and other forms of discriminatory
behaviour. These incidents may arise due to stereotyping – once again, including
stereotypes related to so-called criminality (see [2.3.1]).

       I was approached by a [tram] ticket inspector, before I could take my headphones
       out of my ear she started saying "if you don't have a ticket, you'll have to get off at
       the next stop". I didn't even get time to pull my ticket out when she started saying
       "we all know you don't have a ticket". I asked her if she could step back from me
       because she was intimidating me & I've also been diagnosed with social anxiety
       disorder which she was triggering. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       Every month, [First Nations people contributing to a research project] experience
       racism by taxi drivers when attending [the workplace], although a staff member of
       the [workplace] arranges the taxi pick up and drop off. Examples of racist
       behaviour; demanding payment before taxi leaves, place of pick up, constantly

                                             41
       arriving late e.g. by 30-40mins, not listening to passenger … the important work
       they do, disrespectful behaviour. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

The reports related to transport portray this as an unsafe (public) space for First Nations
people – where racism might be perpetrated by transport providers (see other examples
in this report of racist conversations held with providers), the public or perhaps
experienced as images left on public transport.

       Sitting in [named airline] business lounge, and had a gentleman openly say
       "fucking Abos, wish we should have never voted for the 68 Referendum (in
       response to [named First Nations female senator]). (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

       Me and my siblings booked a ride … through [named ride service], the driver
       initiated a conversation about the history of Australia. They recommended a book
       which supposedly details what happened, and when I asked whether the author
       is Indigenous, she said, 'well he's a 6th generation Aussie so he considers himself
       to be Indigenous' and when I responded, 'so he's not truly Indigenous then' they
       felt the need to tell me 'there's no true Indigenous'. The driver then proceeded to
       spew inaccurate information about the history of Tasmania framing the Aboriginal
       people from that region as savages. (Self-report, Aboriginal)

       I've had many [run-ins] with racism … On a bus there was Aboriginal flags with
       knifes and under the flag drawing was a caption saying fuck black people we need
       to breed it out. So many other experiences. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Very similar incidents to those above are reported in commercial spaces, including
exclusion.

       Owner refused to sign up for basics card, stating "it's not the clientele I want in
       this store". (Witness report, not identified)

Often the same stereotyping is also evident too. There were numerous reports. Including
the following, about First Nations people being treated like criminals in commercial
spaces. See also discussion of barriers to calling racism out at [3.3] and targeting of
young people at [4.3] in this location.

       Asking a dark skinned person to pay first before they provide the ice cream while
       2 light skinned white fellows got ice cream before they pay in front of the dark
       skinned person. Called out loudly to ‘pay first’. (Self-report, not identified)

       Shop Assistant rudely asked an Elder if she could pay for her groceries before she
       unpacked. 'You pay for that'? (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

       Shop owner instructed staff to "treat every blackfella like a perpetrator" and follow
       them when entering the shop. (Witness report, not identified)



                                            42
        During check out at [named supermarket chain] [named town, NT] friend was
        targeted by the [supermarket] worker and who [also] receipt checked me, asking
        if I had paid when clearly had. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal and Torres Strait
        Islander)

Being rendered invisible in commercial spaces was also reported; for instance, as
follows.

        Walked into [named shop, WA], the worker didn't say anything to me at all, I
        browsed for a bit as I was looking for a particular handbag and to also see if the
        worker would assist and do their job. Still didn't get a "hello" or "can I help you with
        anything" and it made me feel so uncomfortable going in there and I will never
        walk into that [shop] ever again. I work hard for my money and just wanted to
        spend it like every other person. I was a customer [and they] treated me like I was
        invisible. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

As a further example of exclusion from public spaces, see discussion of young Aboriginal
people being excluded from a public pool at [2.4.4].23 At [3] and [4] we describe the
impacts of and responses to racism as including avoidance of places/people associated
with racism. These are further examples of shunning/exclusion.

2.4.3 Racism in the workplace

Racism in the workplace has consistently been identified as a significant issue in our
annual reports. For 2024-2025, the workplace is the second most common location for
racism overall (11%) and is proportionally higher for self-reports (15%). Further, 11% of
ongoing incidents occurred in the workplace (see Table 6 in Appendix A). All types of
racism were reported as associated with the workplace (see Table 8 in Appendix A).
Negative attitudes and stereotyping, bullying and intimidation, laws, policies and
practices, cultural rights, and shunning and exclusing were all frequently mentioned.

Workplace related reports spoke of under-employment of First Nations people. This was
called out in the tourism industry, for instance (including where destinations include
culturally significant sites).

        There appears to be systematic exclusion of local Aboriginal people from
        employment in [named town] - with a small number of exceptions, tour guides
        and hotel staff were from dozens of different countries or European descent
        Australians from the East Coast …I spent a week in [named town] recently and
        completed a number of day tours and attended other local sites, museums etc.
        With a small number of exceptions, there were almost no Aboriginal Australians
        employed in any public facing businesses. This included tour guides, hotel staff,

23
  There is discussion in [4] of young people disengaging from school following racism, relevant to
shunning/exclusion though not to discussion of the locations that are the focus of [2.4.2].

                                                   43
       taxi drivers, museums, day tours to [named sacred site]. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

Many reports, however, focused on racism during employment, with a broad range of
issues called out - including limited opportunity for promotion.

       A white woman in a position of power denied a First Nations woman a promotion
       due to jealousy and used racial and gendered stereotypes in her performance
       report. She then scheduled an HR meeting to de-escalate the situation during
       NAIDOC week and had no awareness of this being an issue. (Friend/Relative
       report, non-Indigenous)

We again see stereotyping and aggressive racism (hate speech, verbal abuse) in
workplace incidents. For example,

       My manager is a racist woman that openly discussed me and said, "as she is
       Aboriginal, we can just expect her to go walkabout even when she should be at
       work". (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       I've always been very open about being very insecure about how white my skin is
       to my co workers, I work in an Aboriginal Identified position off country and its one
       of my biggest insecurities. A few weeks ago I dyed my hair and my co-worker
       mentions almost every day since how I'm really "connecting to my Anglo-Saxon
       roots" and pointing out how it matches my "Irish skin tone". I've mentioned that it
       makes me feel more insecure when comments like this are made, but she keeps
       going and even points it out to other co-workers. I know it sounds silly, but she just
       doesn't stop. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       When discussing factors that may affect the Aboriginal community we are
       providing the workplace service to, my non-Indigenous co-worker refers to
       Aboriginal people as coons, gins, blackfellas, blackies, black cunts. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

Other incidents spoke of undermining of the capability of senior First Nations staff,
including in terms of leadership. The second quote also speaks to difficulties of
challenging racism in the workplace and the likely repercussions of doing so (see further
at [3.4]).

       I had a senior position in a corporate and was discussing professional
       development with my supervisor who denied my request and stated: I know you
       are seen as a leader in your community but we need to teach you to be a corporate
       leader. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)




                                            44
       I was asked to set [a] meeting for Aboriginal staff to look at a new training program
       and to provide feedback. This happened and racism was raised. The director was
       so angry when she read the minutes, which [were] not ratified but another non-
       Aboriginal manager sent them to the director but didn't tell me - so when the
       director was angry - I was at a loss as to why she sent an email and included extra
       non-Aboriginal leaders asking for their opinion about ‘the leader’ in the room and
       her ability to control. The leader was me. I called the director the next day and told
       her I didn't appreciate her inferring I wasn't a good leader - she became angry
       again and started saying I am not operating at a level 5 and went on with a lot more
       - following that email the other managers started [to] get angry - one non-
       Aboriginal manager told me what cultural was and both myself and a cultural
       consultant were put in our place [to not] say anything - this is a small part of the
       racism I have faced . (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

This last report and the one that follows refer to the silencing of First Nations voices in
the workplace. The report below also identifies other forms of shunning and exclusion in
this setting, including as loss of work. Indeed the workplace was the most commonly
reported location for shunning/exclusion (15%, Table 8 in Appendix A).

       White collar exclusion from team meetings ... As a contractor to the [named
       federal government agency/service], my supervisor and reporting line learned of
       my background. Since the Voice referendum, I have been excluded from all team
       meetings and input to the function of the team, while other contractors were
       allowed to participate. In those meetings, the team structures and budgets were
       decided, ultimately resulting in the termination of my contract. I have viewed the
       team documents that confirm the push out of my position but will get punished if
       I leak internal documents. (Self-report, Torres Strait Islander male)

Reports indicate that First Nations employees may be targeted by other employees, but
may also witness racism targeting other First Nations people, evidenced in reports above
regarding the racist behaviour of health staff towards First Nations patients (see [2.3.3]).
Non-Indigenous third party reports also identified incidents witnessed in a workplace
setting.

       I work as a psychologist, and I opened a discussion with my clinical supervisor
       (also a psychologist) about culturally appropriate psychometric measures to use
       with First Nations clients. My supervisor stated, "don't worry about that, you won’t
       get many of them here". (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

       [We] are conducting [an AI program] pilot at our workplace. We have a site to
       share learnings. One of the pilot participants posted that he asked [the AI
       program] a question about alcoholism in Indigenous communities and that it
       wouldn't answer the question (including the screen shots of his prompt and the
       responses). It is not related to our workplace, or the reasons we are running a 3

                                            45
       month pilot program to understand how our workplace can utilise AI to improve
       efficiency. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

School/educational settings were one of the more commonly identified locations for
racism reported to the Register (10%, see Figure 6), including reports about university
employment such as the following.

       Racism toward me as someone with mixed heritage. Believes in a caste system
       and treated me as inferior and even questioned my race and cultural authority …
       My employer treated me poorly based on my race and spread rumours about my
       Aboriginal identity to damage my career and reputation as he was in competition
       with me in academia and worked actively to keep me behind in my career.
       casualised me and then re-advertised my position despite high performance and
       student satisfaction and research outputs. Excluded me from important cultural
       and social and research events where I continue to take a lead. Made jokes about
       my private life and continued to harass me in the roles I took on in other
       organisations. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

As a further example, one First Nations woman reported starting work at a university in a
professorial and managerial position, successfully bringing in grant monies and staff and
working collaboratively with colleagues. She was told to surrender some of her funding
as the university was ‘in trouble’ and was also prevented from backfilling a staff position.
Other events followed.

       I then started to notice that each time I organised a meeting with a senior
       bureaucrat that my EA had notified senior people who arranged for particular
       white folk or staff to turn up to my meetings without my knowledge. I do not
       understand why. I travelled interstate to attend a meeting with the Premier's chief
       of staff to discuss curriculum for First Nations Youth in Detention. I was asked by
       my supervisor why he had not been included. I told him he had not been invited.
       He then notified me that he believed I was not there for University work when [he]
       knew I was. After taking my funding and policing my movements I realised that I
       was being discriminated against. He had arranged meetings with my staff (all
       white) without my knowledge. I thought up until then that I had enjoyed a good
       working relationship with all my staff and am an experienced manager and know
       that staff are my most important asset. Sadly, my boss had convinced them to
       turn on me. Comments were made about the inadequacies of local Aboriginal
       people (compared to those in traditional communities) which made it clear that
       Eastern side Aboriginal people are not as 'real' as those in traditional
       communities. I found that confronting. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)




                                            46
2.4.4 Criminal legal system

The Register received multiple reports this year about racism within the criminal legal
system. Racism occurring in a ‘“justice”/legal setting (e.g. policing, court or prison)’
accounted for 6% of all reports made to the Register in 2024-25 (see Figure 6 above and
Table 6 in Appendix A).24 Incidents occurring in a legal setting are discussed in other
sections of the report (for example, [2.3.3]) and as they relate to young people, at [4.3].

A particular focus this year is on incidents involving police responses to First Nations
peoples as victims of crime. A self-report received from an Aboriginal man who was a
victim of an assault recounted one such incident, describing police failure to investigate
the crime in question.

        I am 66 years of age, as is my cousin. We were attacked in public hotel by an
        intoxicated person (non-Indigenous stranger); security asked us to leave. We
        asked them to call the police; we asked police to check cameras of the incident.
        There has been no follow up of the incident despite us asking for the camera to be
        checked and that we wanted to press charges. The police were very dismissive,
        and we felt we were stereotyped as being the "Aboriginal problem". Rang to
        request incident event number the next day, text to me 2 days after. I again asked
        if the cameras had been checked, no response or contact has been made to me.
        I had bruising on both arms and my leg where the intoxicated person man handled
        me and pushed me. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

This incident, including failure to investigate, clearly resulted in both physical and
psychological harm, and created another layer of victimisation. The victim already had
issues with policing in his local area and now has lost all confidence in police (see also
below at [3.2]).

        Depressed, and sore and bruised where I was manhandled. I'm extra cautious of
        my surroundings … Local police often harass and over police Aboriginal people in
        my locale, I have lost all confidence in them. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

A further report was made by a First Nations victim of a serious assault by an intoxicated
non-Indigenous male on a licenced premises, leading to the loss of his front teeth. His
report addressed police failure to investigate the assault, with police refusing to
differentiate between victim and perpetrator. Systemic racial bias and presumption of
guilt were evident in his report.




24
  While only two percentage points higher compared to 2023-24, the actual number of reports indicating
racism in a legal setting almost doubled – increasing from 23/573 (or 4%) in 2023-24 to 45/703 (or 6%) in
2024-25.

                                                   47
       A white man was racially taunting a [European] man and made a derogatory
       remark about black people knowing I would hear it. I stepped in and said "There's
       no need for racist remarks" to which the white man suddenly and unexpectedly
       hit me in the mouth loosening my four front teeth. The security officer called the
       police. When the police arrived the white man and I were both fined for violence
       in a licensed premises and public nuisance. I informed the police that I had been
       the victim and to check the CCTV footage as I had not touched the man at all. The
       police refused to check the footage or investigate further. I am now taking the
       matter to court. The police automatically assumed I must have instigated the
       incident or retaliated. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

The immediate assumption made by police – that the victim was in fact the instigator –
demonstrates clearly the stereotype that First Nations people are inherently violent or
confrontational, subsequently resulting in the victim being criminalised. He further
described how the incident has impacted him both physically and financially.

       I have seen the dentist who cannot save my front teeth and I am wearing the cost
       of dentures now and legal fees to go to court. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

One detailed report provided by an Aboriginal woman, which may be difficult to read,
provides essential insight into how racism and police practices still cause harm for First
Nations people. The detailed incident describes the use of excessive force on a young
child by a security guard and police at a shopping centre. The woman filmed the incident,
highlighting her resilience and advocacy to hold police and security accountable for their
actions towards a young child in a public place.

       This morning at [the] shopping centre there was a security guard abusing a 9 year
       old child. The main female abuser who was assaulting the child, did not have her
       badge number displayed and refused to show identification. They did not like
       [that] I was filming. Every living man/woman has the duty to help their fellow
       humans and has a right to film a crime happening. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Her action of filming the incident subsequently led to the attention of police and she was
arrested. She shared further the trauma she experienced of her arrest and in police
custody of physical harm and verbal abuse.

       When 6ft police officer came. He also assaulted the child. The child was crying
       and he was twisting his arm. The child was screaming and asking him to stop. The
       officer stated he did not consent to being filmed and was extremely intimidating.
       He then went on a crazy tirade of abuse and stated I was trespassing and he would
       sort me out. He would have me banned and then forcefully removed my phone
       from me stating he was taking it for evidence and then he said I was under arrest
       and then bent my arm back and took me to the police beat. He then continued his



                                           48
       abuse and yelling, stating things like, he was going to make my life hell and he
       would be taking me to court to make me pay. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

She further recounts police failure to follow protocol when First Nations people are in
custody and describes institutional neglect of duty of care, failure to appropriately
respond to medical needs, and dehumanising police practices of invasive searching and
physical harm.

       I have complex PTSD and I had a panic attack and asthma attack [in custody].
       [Police officer] refused to call an ambulance. I threw up whilst laying on the floor
       where he then kicked me and said stop being aggressive. His female colleague
       then came who searched me and my belongings and laughed and joked about
       woman going through DV and PTSD. And woman being murdered. They did call an
       ambulance. I asked the officers to write their names down and they refused. I
       asked them to call the officer in charge as I did not feel safe. They refused. I asked
       them to call the Aboriginal liaison officer and they refused. They then said they
       weren't waiting for the ambulance and were taking me to the watch house. They
       assaulted me again, hitting my arm and pushing me into the van. The female
       officer searched me in front of male officers. She put her hand inside my bra and
       underpants. They turned the air conditioning off and laughed when I said I couldn't
       breathe. And they joked that maybe I will die. They did not take me to the watch
       house. The left me in the van for what felt like 15-20 minutes. When the
       ambulance arrived, I was dehydrated as the police refused to give me water and I
       had a very high temperature as well as very high heart rate. (Self-report, Aboriginal
       female)

This same woman describes what happened when she made a complaint about the
incident.

       I still have zero help with this racist cop and police are ignoring my complaints as
       usual. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Another report by an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander man identified systemic racial
bias cycling across generations as well as the psychological impact and the provocation
for his family of over-policing when responding to minor matters.

       Living in a small community there is always a risk of running into the police. My
       wife was chased in our car and pulled over; the police thought it was me. Because
       I had no licence, she took the car to work. They question her about me? Five police
       officers came to my house to talk to my son about trafficking a couple of grams of
       pot. 5 of them just to talk to him. Talk about provocation. Made my stomach
       churn, felt distressed. (Self-report, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander male)




                                            49
Another non-Indigenous witness report addressed racism where police extinguished
ceremonial fire and removed tools at Camp Sovereignty. Police actions, from the witness
account, were culturally insensitive in misunderstanding the importance of the camp
and disregarding cultural protocols attached to sacred practices. The report again
captures the systemic actions of racism and bias in law enforcement. 25

        I first heard of this matter when I attended a public hearing at the Federal Court
        between an Indigenous activist and the State over claims that a sacred fire in
        Kings Domain, where Indigenous activists gather as part of 'Camp Sovereignty',
        had been extinguished. The police had supposedly entered Camp Sovereignty
        and extinguished the fire, whilst also confiscating numerous fire tools from the
        site. These items were allegedly returned, however the principal of the matter
        demonstrates the misunderstanding and inherent bias by the police and the state
        of Aboriginal culture and the value they place on sacred fires such as this. As the
        fire is a symbol for a continuing fight against ending genocide, acknowledging
        sovereignty and a securing a treaty. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

A non-Indigenous witness reported racism at a regional swimming pool – where police
actions were influenced by stereotypes, causing the misuse of police powers. Police
were called to the pool because of the behaviour of a few children. Instead of the pool
staff addressing the specific behaviour of the individual children, police proceeded to
remove all Aboriginal children.

        Staff called police because a couple of kids were playing 'unsafe' and were 'rude'
        to staff. Police forced all Aboriginal people, around 20 and mostly kids, to leave
        the pool, including by serving move on orders. The remaining White children were
        not asked to leave or removed. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Of critical importance, according to the witness report, these actions reproduce similar
patterns of exclusion – reminding the families connected to this incident that the
historical denial of access to public spaces persists and how past exclusions via racist
laws are reproduced in present-day police practices.




25
  See media release from Senator Malarndirri McCarthy calling out the recent racist attacks on Camp
Sovereignty (in 2025) during the anti-immigration rallies around the country and claims that police did not
do enough to protect Aboriginal people: <https://ministers.pmc.gov.au/mccarthy/2025/senate-
statement-camp-sovereignty>.

                                                    50
2.5    When the racism was experienced or witnessed

2.5.1 Single and multiple incidents of racism

Reports to Call It Out often contain multiple incidents of racism experienced or
witnessed by the same person – sometimes occurring over many years and across
generations. This means that the overall number of reports we identify as having been
made to Call It Out are a significant undercount of incidents reported.

This new optional question was answered by
most respondents (369/442 or 83%). Of these
369 respondents, just under half indicated
that their report included multiple incidents
of racism (172/369 or 47%), with the
remainder being single incidents (see Figure
7 and Table 9 in Appendix A). Perhaps not
surprisingly,     First   Nations     people
experiencing racism directly were more likely
to report multiple incidents of racism (54%)
compared to friends/relatives (44%) and
witnesses (43%) (see Table 9 in Appendix A).

As an example of how people responded to
this question, one First Nations woman
identified that she was reporting ‘multiple
incidents’ in sport, beginning with the
following.

       The Caucasian team manager said so you are a half caste and where do you get
       your colour from one parent or both. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

She then reports being turned down for a managerial position with her sports team.

       I had a call on the following Monday and was told they made a mistake as League
       Manager is a paid position and said they will be doing that role and I won't be
       required. I said I was happy to give back and support women in sport and was not
       doing it for the money and was happy to volunteer. I told now operations manager
       about incident but nothing happened she kept her role and I was let go. (Self-
       report, Aboriginal female)

She goes on to state that this is just one incident among many, including others related
to education, and describes the repercussions for her children following the above
incidents directed at her (see further discussion at [4.5]).




                                          51
2.5.2 When the racism happened

Those completing the Register were also asked to indicate when the incident happened,
including whether it was ‘ongoing’. This optional question was answered by 79% of all
respondents (or 348/442, see Table 10 in Appendix A).

As shown in Figure 8, more than half of
all reported incidents occurred
‘recently (in the last three months)’
(56%). Almost a quarter of incidents
were identified as occurring on an
ongoing basis (22%). All three groups
reporting to the Register were
proportionately more likely to identify
recent incidents. Friend/relative
reports and self-reports were
proportionately more likely to identify
ongoing racism (33% and 27%,
respectively) compared to witness
reports (18%). (See Table 10 in
Appendix A).

Further analysis of reports of ongoing racism indicates the following.

   ● Social media or online incidents were most frequently nominated as the location
     for ongoing racism (23%), followed by school/educational setting (12%), the
     workplace (11%) and public setting (10%) (see Table 11 in Appendix A).
   ● The types of racism most frequently nominated as ongoing were negative
     attitudes or stereotyping (25%), followed by verbal abuse or hate speech (16%),
     discriminatory laws, policies and practices and not recognising cultural rights
     (both 14%), and bullying, threats or intimidation (13%) (see Table 12 in Appendix
     A). We note that in combination, aggressive racism constitutes 35% of all ongoing
     racism (see also [2.3.2] above).

2.5.3 Incidence of racism – general comments

As we have consistently recorded in previous Call It Out reporting, racism targeting First
Nations people is entrenched, endemic and hard to accurately capture statistically -
though the Register questions about whether incidents are ongoing or reported as
multiple or single incidents go some way to doing this.
We again see reports of single incidents with multiple layers and multiple incidents
occurring in different locations.



                                           52
       I've experienced racism on a daily basis going to a shop or school or getting my
       hair cut to doing shopping or speaking on phone to Centrelink. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

       So, I was walking home … when a guy [drove] past and called me a monkey and
       other forms of obscenities … I [also] experienced racism about 4 months ago, in
       [a convenience store] where a [South Asian] guy refused me service even though
       I had money, but yet? Still refused me service & he only served white people but
       not people like me who have dark skin. Not only that but this has been an ongoing
       problem on different occasions, where I experienced racism that includes when I
       … went for a job interview with the army the guy was being very prejudiced and
       racist, it also includes in the gyms I go to, & when I go to the shops, or walking on
       the street minding my own business. It has gotten out of control now where
       something has to be done! (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

Racism was identified in the Register as tied to history too - again in keeping with previous
annual reporting. Reports referencing intergenerational experiences of racism or harmful
government policy or stereotyping drawing from the past into the present day are
examples. Examples include the incident involving the taxi driver using the term ‘natives’,
references to ‘half-castes’, how exclusion of young Aboriginal people from a public pool
brings up similar past exclusion and the following reports.

       The ongoing colonial loading of a westernised Government workplace is a
       reminder that daily experiences of racism is an essential [criterion] within your
       identified … role. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       I was in our local [named supermarket chain] yesterday with a gift card, and the
       employer asked me if it was a Mission Card … I am very angry. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

Also demonstrating the multiple layers of discrimination experienced by First Nations
people, some reports to the Register identify intersectionality between race and other
bases for unequal treatment. One First Nations person reported the following statement
‘"never met a gay Aboriginal before"’ and their response to this comment as ‘CUZ GO
EDUCATE YOURSELF’ (self-report, Aboriginal).

As another example, a First Nations person reported various grounds of discrimination
in their employment at a university.

       When I commenced a new role in the university sector, I was treated with
       prejudice based on my mixed race heritage and my appearance, in the Indigenous
       space. I was bullied, harassed, and intimidated even in my own home after I left
       the role after HR got involved, because another Indigenous employee (from a
       country other than Australia) was a neighbour, and bullied me and intimidated me
       at work and in my own home. I was also subject to homophobia and political

                                             53
        discrimination for my role in a referendum campaign calling for a First Nations
        constitutional voice. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

The broad range of perpetrators reported to the Register, to which we turn now, also
evidences the multiple levels and contexts in which racism arises for First Nations
people.

2.6     Perpetrators of racism

Those completing the Register were
asked to nominate the type of
perpetrator of the racism reported
from 6 different options. This was a
compulsory question and notably,
multiple responses were made by 113
individuals (n=625, see Table 13 in
Appendix A).

As Figure 9 shows, the two most
commonly identified perpetrators
were ‘a stranger’ (26%) and
‘employee/worker’ (25%).26 The third
most commonly identified perpetrator
was ‘institution or organisation as a
whole’ (20%).27 (See also Table 13 in
Appendix A).28

Witnesses most frequently identified
the perpetrator as a stranger, and this is likely, as noted above at [2.4.1], because
witnesses more frequently reported racism on social media/online – with perpetrators
described, for instance as ‘just a faceless person online’ (self-report, Aboriginal female).
All groups reported ‘institutions and organisations as a whole’ as a perpetrator at a
similar frequency. (See Table 13 in Appendix A).

Notably, First Nations people directly experiencing racism and friends/relatives were
much more likely than witnesses, comparatively, to identify the perpetrator as an
employee/worker (by a difference of 12 and 13 percentage points, respectively) or as

As a further example of known perpetrators, one First Nations woman reported a
member of her church congregation.
       A member of the parish council of our local church approached myself and my

The significant size and scope of the problem that is racism is again revealed this year by
the range of perpetrators reported to the Register, including across different genders,
social groups and various ethnicities. A relatively high proportion of responses identified
multiple perpetrators, including for single incidents. One witness described perpetrators
of an online/media incident related to a hit and run of a young First Nations woman as
multi-layered, as but one example.

       Media: Misidentifying a hit and run victim as a 'crash' victim by mainstream media,
       [named newspaper, QLD] on Facebook. Factually incorrect and implies the victim
       was involved/to blame somehow. Police: Apparent failure to properly investigate
       by police. No surprises there. General public: Many responded to the post with
       laughing emojis. Inciting one person to respond 'why are people laughing at this.
       shame on you'. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Similarly, perpetrators involved in excluding First Nations children from the NSW pool
were identified as ‘Pool staff, police and non-Indigenous bystanders who said nothing,
did nothing’ (witness report, non-Indigenous).

Figure 12 shows that more than

over a quarter as male (26%).31 A significant proportion of respondents identified the
gender of the victim as ‘not applicable’ (31%). The ’not applicable’ category could arise,
for example, with racist comments in social or mainstream media that target and impact
First Nations people as a group. (See also Table 19 in Appendix A).

2.7.2 Age of the victim

More than two thirds of people
filling in the Register answered the
optional question on the age of the

person subjected to the racism was aged 40 or over.32

Notably, in 2024-25 more than a quarter of reported incidents (26%) targeted children
and young people in the 0-19 age group. This represents an increase of 10 percentage
points compared with 2023-24.33 (See Table 20 in Appendix A).

We also examined the age group of the victim by the type of racism experienced or
witnessed. There was little difference across age groups, with negative
attitudes/stereotypes and verbal abuse/hate speech being proportionately the most
prevalent type of racism for all ages. However, children and young people (0-19 age
group) were subjected somewhat more frequently to bullying, threats or intimidation (5-
8 percentage points difference) and physical harm (4-6 percentage points) (see Table 21
in Appendix A).

3. Responses to Racism
Questions on the Call It Out Register asked how the person reporting racism felt about it,
identifying its emotional impacts, and whether and how they responded or took action in
response to racism. Sharing of perspectives on more effective responses to racism were
also invited.

3.1     Impacts of racism

Those completing the Register were
asked to nominate how they felt
about the incident reported from a
range of 14 options. In 2024-25, a
maximum of three responses could
be nominated for this question.39
Some 314 (71%) of the 442 people
completing the Register chose to
answer this question. The majority of
this group (272) indicated multiple
responses (n=832, see Table 27 in
Appendix A).

As shown in Figure 18, the most
common feeling identified by all
groups was anger (22%), followed by
disappointment (14%), frustration
(13%) and motivation to bring about
change (11%).40 (See also Table 27 in
Appendix A).

Perhaps unsurprisingly, those who
self-reported and friends/relatives
were proportionately more likely to
feel humiliation (11% and 8%,

3.1.1 Emotional impacts

The experiences recorded on the Register show that a multitude of different emotions are
experienced by those targeted by or witnessing racism – and often all at once. As
examples, the First Nations person who reported her manager as saying she’d go
‘walkabout’ felt anger, isolation, sadness and fear.

        I am scared that I will lose my job because the new manager openly hates me. I
        am now working less to try and avoid her which has caused financial difficulties
        for me and my family. I am also angry that someone in a position of power and
        employed in a government role is so openly racist and horrible without concern,
        sad that things are still so far behind reality, isolated and alone cos I'm the only
        Aboriginal employee in the team. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

The First Nations person who encountered and challenged racism during a beauty
treatment also reported a range of emotions.

        It made me feel all sorts of feelings, even guilty for not being able to change his
        perspective. Hopeless that even nice people haven't learnt who we are.
        It made what should have been a nice self-care experience feel tiring. Made me
        sad for my grandchildren and worried what they will experience. (Self-report,
        Aboriginal)




41
  Note the number of available response options changed in 2024-25, increasing from 8 to 11 options.

internal HR)’; ‘Disengaged (e.g. walked away, took a break from social media)’; ‘Other action (e.g.
reported to media, wrote a letter)’; and ‘Avoided the place/person (e.g. didn't go back to shop/service,
left my job/studies)’.

As discussed above, emotions more commonly reported are anger and frustration –
including for the First Nations woman encountering racism in a local sauna and those
witnessing the fishing competition interview.

       Well unfortunately I am not surprised at all. I have heard it all before too many
       times over my life. It pissed me off that I can't even go to the local [sauna] …
       without hearing this type of bullshit. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       Angry. Empty. Sad for something finally positive for our culture to be tainted and
       aggressively done. Constantly shame. Always trying to prove ourselves. Very, very
       angry. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Incidents like the latter that arise online or in the media may lead to emotional responses
across First Nations communities, including and beyond witnesses reporting it to Call It
Out. The two reports below again discuss the fishing competition interview. The first
report speaks of racist comments posted online by the public in response to a TikTok
video calling this interview out (see also above at [2.4.1]).

       The commenter wasn't just targeting this Indigenous TikTok creator, they were
       also targeting Indigenous people as a whole as they were stereotyping [them]. I'm
       trying not to let it negatively affect me too much, but it's so hard, and I know I
       should be focusing my energy to do good things. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

       This impacts not only the young man from [named town], but 3% of the population
       in this Country - including Me. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Other emotions described in reports were fear (3%) and concern more broadly, including
for First Nations people living in communities openly expressing race-based hatred and
hostility on social media. ‘I'm worried they are going to try and start a civil war. They are
all talking about it’ (self-report, Aboriginal female).

Isolation and distrust were also reported, including where nobody steps in to challenge
racism - as was the case for the First Nations employee working alongside a racist
student nurse. This was also raised by an Aboriginal witness to racism online.

       It made me feel uncomfortable and quite apprehensive to work alongside this
       person. I was also disappointed that none of my colleagues challenged her.
       (Witness report, Aboriginal)

       Hurts seeing this all the time and others jump on there [online] and agree but no
       one goes on there to stand up to him. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Distrust was raised by the First Nations woman assaulted in a public hotel and who
received a poor response to the incident from police (above at [2.4.4]). Problematic
policing more generally can lead to distrust.



                                             66
       I'm extra cautious of my surroundings and not confident in police providing any
       assistance in these types of circumstances. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       Local police often harass and over-police Aboriginal people in my locale, I have
       lost all confidence in them. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Shame was experienced by non-Indigenous people witnessing racism, including after
witnessing First Nations people being excluded from a bus. ‘I am deeply ashamed and so
very sorry that these four passengers were treated like this’ (witness report, non-
Indigenous). As a further example,

       Shame (about my own non-Indigenous people). I was also angry at what a
       complete idiot this woman was; she was telling someone she thought was
       Aboriginal to go back to a land they're inherently from. First Nations and non-
       Indigenous people are working so hard together to create a brighter future and
       idiots like her can ruin people's day in one fell swoop. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

For First Nations people, shame or humiliation was reported following security guard
attention in stores and, as the following comment indicates, during the incident when
the older First Nations woman was prevented from sharing a seat on a train platform. This
report also describes the exhaustion experienced due to ongoing racism.

       The victim is older, has health conditions and is a very respected member of her
       community. It's humiliating to be treated with obvious disrespect and distain.
       It's just that ongoing feeling of exhaustion from the weight of racism.
       Wears you down. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

Sadness was felt by the First Nations person who was made to feel not ‘Blak’ enough at
work.

       Feeling pretty frustrated at work, impacts professional relationship and makes
       me feel too "white" to be in an Identified position. I walk around paranoid,
       everyone is questioning whether I'm Blak or not just because of my skin. I don’t
       like wearing my hair out and want to change it now. After a few weeks of things
       building I just sit in my car at the end of the day and cry because I feel like I have
       to prove myself every second of the day. I thought after 30 years I was starting to
       feel comfortable in my own skin, but not anymore. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

And also, by the First Nations man made to feel invisible while shopping, who again
describes the cumulative effect of ongoing racism.

       I felt depressed after that. I know some may think it's a minor thing but that small
       act made a big impact on me and my mental well-being coz it is not an isolated
       incident for Blak fullas. We have to deal with this almost daily! (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

                                            67
Related to this sadness and exhaustion are emotional responses of helplessness and
despair - sometimes following more immediate responses such as shock or anger. The
witness who reported the child protection system identified being ‘continually shocked
but now sadly not surprised’ by the ‘widespread racism’ in question. ‘Completely in
despair that it is supposed to be a 'protection' system for our children’ (witness report,
non-Indigenous).

The witness who described negative audience feedback on an Acknowledgement of
Country identified this as having ‘contributed to my sense of Australia's social cohesion
becoming undermined due to organised hate and disinformation campaigns. I'm losing
faith in Australia's capacity and willingness to improve things for us all’. This feeling is
more pronounced when there seems to be no remedy for racism. ‘I had to accept that I
had no recourse for calling out the racism. The choice was to simply ignore it...’ (witness
report, non-Indigenous).

One First Nations person who left a government job working on Country due to racism
reported feeling ‘like there’s no help for Aboriginal people’, as well as thinking about self-
harming (self-report, Aboriginal male). Another First Nations person identified racism as
a ‘silencer’ (self-report, Aboriginal female), a point raised earlier in discussion of
workplace racism.

For some, being in some sense ‘resigned’ to racism was a protective response, as was
the case for two First Nations people reporting workplace incidents – and again, this
occurs in particular where there is a belief that nothing can be done about racism.

       I am so used to this type of behaviour, it is the normal. Sometimes I think just
       accept it and keep moving on, if I stop and try to address it, it always comes back
       to bite me and I lose my job and sanity. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       … now knowing that because it’s a government department that has a lot of
       resources, I can't do anything about it, accept move on and face the fact that
       things will never change. I've had to deal with this my whole life. Calling it out but
       the black man has no say! (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

Others spoke of being motivated to bring about change and/or feeling solidarity with
those encountering racism. As one First Nations woman states in describing being
repeatedly asked to provide proof of purchase at a hardware store (when non-Indigenous
people didn’t have to do this), ‘Ongoing racism towards myself or my people is
unacceptable and is not tolerated by me’ (self-report, Aboriginal female).

Witnesses also described similar responses. The person who was called an ‘<n word>
lover’ for calling out Australia Day to a family member stated that this ‘made me angry
and even more motivated to speak up against the racism around me, especially in white
spaces’ (witness report, non-Indigenous). Another stated, ‘Will continue to support


                                             68
Aboriginal people [in my work] to lead solutions to racism and over incarceration as a key
manifestation of racism’ (friend/relative report, non-Indigenous).

3.1.2 Other impacts of racism

Further impacts on socio-economic, cultural and other forms of wellbeing were reported
to the Register. The significant physical and psychological health implications of racism
were highlighted, in particular. As noted in previous annual reporting, these arise both
during and following an incident, including due to poor responses to challenges to
racism, and can be long-term in nature. Some of the accounts in [3.1.1] describe
significant emotional impacts, including thoughts of self-harm, for instance. As other
examples, the first report below relates to a First Nations man being discriminated
against while flying (including being removed from a flight, with police attending) and the
second to a workplace incident.

       My mental health has taken a big blow and I have been recently diagnosed from
       this incident as having PTSD. I experience panic attacks near or around airports,
       flight attendants and planes. I am also terrified of men in uniform (such as police).
       I've taken time off work as I cannot function. I am teary all the time and cry a lot.
       I've lost hope in people which I had previously and I cannot trust anymore. My
       whole world has changed and tilted on its axis and I have no confidence that this
       will get any better, despite receiving ongoing psychological support. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

       I am so anxious, feeling like a failure. I don't want to go to work as I have
       headaches every day and don't sleep well as I always wake up. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

One friend reported another perpetrating racism against his Aboriginal ‘mate’, calling
him ‘a petrol sniffer and a dumb abo’ and ‘discriminating against him because of his
race’. ‘[T]hey make him very sad all the time I'm worried about his mental health’ (witness
report, non-Indigenous).

Financial impacts were also reported, including for workplace related incidents. Note
how these impacts have broader consequences (including not being able to make
mortgage and other repayments, according to reports to the Register).

       I ended up struggling to find income after leaving this role and declared
       bankruptcy [… and had] to seek crucial surgery for my teeth which are still in
       immense pain. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

       I lost my main source of income and slowly became bankrupt as he continued to
       bully me and intimidate me and spread racist rumours about me - I had to get a
       new job in a new state - I became depressed, suicidal and ended up experiencing



                                            69
       domestic violence as my life began to fall apart. I have only just begun to recover.
       (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

       As a result, my wife blames me for our financial position and wants to leave me. I
       feel like a failure. My kids wonder why I'm crying all the time. I really thought a
       black man could make it in the corporate world, but the boys-club who pushed
       me out are too sneaky and they're going to get away with it without any problems
       too. (Self-report, Torres Strait Islander male)

Another First Nations man described ‘Loss of job, blocked from getting work … [and
being] financially bankrupt from not being paid wages’ following workplace related
incidents. He also identified as impacts ‘mental, career, reputation, self-esteem,
confidence’ (self-report, Aboriginal male). The First Nations woman who called out the
racism of a charity (successful in accessing funding by bringing her First Nations-led
organisation into a funding application) also identified financial loss, including due to
lost business relationships.

       I have suffered severe financial hardship this year as I had said no to other work
       because of the work I was contracted to [deliver for named charity]. My health has
       been impacted very badly. Jaw clenching causing intense headaches,
       depression, loss of interest in usual activities, crying. I had built business
       relationships for five years and have been isolated from those relationships
       because of calling out racism. (Self-report, Torres Strait Islander female)

       We lost $86k of income for that year. Overall, the opportunity cost to our
       Indigenous business in this [named charity] Charity Fraud was $645,000 over five
       years. Had we not joined the … consortium and submitted our own grant
       application we could have achieved [a] $645,000 grant ourselves as we were the
       only business in the country [able to offer specialised] training to First Nations and
       women of colour [to be funded]. (Self-report, Torres Strait Islander female)

Disconnection from important community ties was also reported, including by the First
Nations woman targeted by a member of her church congregation.

       My children became targets of subtle and kind of covert singling out to a point
       where we no longer go to that church community as a direct result of what
       happened. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Family and friend connections may also be affected, as occurred for the First Nations
woman talking about Uluru with her sister.

       Impacted our relationship as I don't know if I want to continue having a
       relationship with her. My mental health was affected as it left me feeling quite
       depressed and I felt a lot of grief about my family, my dad and about my
       connection to my Indigenous background. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)


                                            70
Homelessness was a further potential impact of racism identified in reports. One First
Nations woman reported racism by her real estate agent but also the courts who
(incorrectly) determined that she could not pay her water or rent bills as tenant. This led
to a court order for eviction.

       [The court] did not check if I had paid the rent and water bill and they went ahead
       and posted on the court order that I did not pay [them]. Which the [real estate]
       staff member must have said in Court. I was told by the manager of [the real
       estate] she would put to the Sherrif’s office that I was to be evicted and it would
       be in the next days because the owners wanted me out and vacant possession. I
       know I didn’t pay rent and water on time but I know the rent and water bills were
       paid.
The practical and emotional impacts of this court order are identified as substantial.

       The Court Order broke me. I cried, I was shaking. My head was spinning. I couldn't
       walk. My blood pressure was over 90 on the reading. I just didn’t know what to do.
       The Courts decision was unfair. I didn’t attend the court because I was sick and
       had difficulty walking. I am afraid of falling down. I have had a brain scan. I have
       blurred vision as well and can’t read small print. The long term impact is that the
       comment made by the Court will influence all possible applications not to grant
       to me a rental property. I would be homeless living on the street, 81 years old all
       my life's collection of items I valued taken by the Sheriffs' [office]. I would lose all
       my paintings, my computer and other items I valued. (Self-report, Aboriginal
       female)

A further report discussing homelessness as an impact is as follows, and as above, one
First Nations person experiencing racist harassment by a neighbour in public housing
reports trying to leave her current home.

       Non Aboriginal neighbour of Aunt is racially abusing her and forcing her to leave
       her public housing unit where she was so happy and safe. (Friend/Relative report,
       non-Indigenous)

3.1.3 Emotional and other impacts of racism for those who self-reported racism,
      by gender

We investigated responses to the question about how the incident made the person feel
by gender of those who self-reported racism. Of this group, more than half (85/155 or
55%) chose to respond to this optional question, and a majority of these (76/85 or 89%)
selected multiple responses (n=231, see Table 29 in Appendix A). In 2024-25,
respondents could select up to a maximum of three responses for this question.

For both men and women, the most frequent feelings were anger (21% males and 18%
females) and disappointment (13% females and 10% males), followed by humiliation


                                             71
(12% females and 10% males), frustration (10% males and 9% females), isolation (9%
females and 6% males) and sadness (8% males and 7% females) (see Table 29 in
Appendix A). Overall, for those who self-reported racism there was very little difference
by gender in feelings arising due to experiences of racism.
