3.2.1 Responding to racism

Our previous reporting identified that many see calling racism out as an essential
strategy for reducing its incidence. This was again the case in 2024-25, with one in five
people (Table 27, Appendix A) identifying feeling motivated to bring about change and/or
solidarity with those who are targeted by this issue.

       It has gotten out of control now where something has to be done! This cannot
       continue and that is why I joined this platform, to speak up for my own rights! & To
       fight for equality & justice & fairness & to be treated like a normal human being.
       (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

People are responding to racism by defending themselves/another (13%, Table 27,
Appendix A). Examples include the two First Nations women; one who recorded on video
the assault on a young person in a store (subsequently arrested by police) and the other
who challenged racism at the sauna.

       I have experienced this type of talk too many times in my life and thought I'd speak
       up and just let them know I am Aboriginal and I don't get everything for free. I
       handled myself well and tried to not show too much anger. It turned into a bit of a
       debate and one of the younger men kind of became an ally to me. I then heard the
       usual spiel of not all Aboriginals are like this etc. I then just proceeded to leave the
       premises and have not returned since - this happened over a year ago. (Self-
       report, Aboriginal female)

                                             73
The following further example describes a First Nations man feeling like retaliating
against family members perpetrating racism but confronting them verbally instead.

       My in-laws were visiting my wife and I and they invited some of their friends over
       for breakfast and their friend made a joke … "it's like culling Aboriginal people". I
       paused and watched him and his wife laughing and my in-laws joining in the
       laughter. I said with a stern voice "I'm Aboriginal". I got a reply "yeah I know" and
       the laughter continued. Until I said that's not right you shouldn't say that. The
       mood changed I had to leave my own home before I assaulted him. I felt like
       dragging him out of my house and hurting him. I didn't. I left and went to my
       mum’s. The next day I confronted my in-laws and they kept interrupting me before
       I could tell them how I felt and it got out of hand they got defensive and started to
       yell and I asked them to leave my home. They call me a Son but they didn't even
       look at [me] when they got home didn't console me didn't ask me if I'm okay. Just
       acted like it didn't happen … (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

When a ‘student voiced in a group setting, should we ask if they are sniffing petroleum?...
during a medical studies lecture and case study work’ the First Nations woman reporting
the incident ‘Questioned their thinking and thought process-smashed the stereotype
publicly’ (self-report, Aboriginal female). In the incident where the First Nations woman
was blocked from sitting down at the train platform both women ‘loudly spoke up
between ourselves within ear shot that it was hurtful and a clear act of racism’
(friend/relative report, Aboriginal).

Direct questioning or confrontation leads to varied and unpredictable outcomes, as is
clear from accounts shared throughout this report. As further examples shared in self-
reports, the first comment below was provided by the First Nations person responding to
her sister’s comments about Uluru, the second relates to the transport incident involving
use of the term ‘natives’, and the third to the racism from a stranger in a bakery. These
examples demonstrate that calling racism out directly in conversation may have
somewhat limited impacts on the attitudes of racists.

       I tried to shut the conversation down, but she started raising her voice at me and
       telling me I'm rigid in my way of thinking about Indigenous people. I told her that
       her views are outdated. She also works for the government which is even more
       disappointing. Husband is in military, and they are complete racists. Older
       generations with brainwashed views. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       I told the driver that calling First Nations peoples "natives" is insulting and that
       maybe things would improve if he referred to us as First Nations people. Second,
       not all our people are homeless, violent, etc. I told him that it was insulting for him
       to assume these negative thoughts of us. He then decided to tell me I was too fair
       to be a native. I asked him when he makes coffee, if he adds milk, does he still call
       it coffee? Before he could answer, I politely requested that we cease our

                                             74
       conversation I was upset by his comments and was no longer interested in
       continuing the conversation. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       I turned around and told him his comments were offensive and unnecessary.
       Instead of taking a moment to reflect, he started yelling at me, claiming that "no
       one wants to talk about the problems." It was clear he wasn't open to reasoning,
       so I decided to leave … What kind of world do we live in? (Self-report, Aboriginal
       female)

Witnesses also spoke about stepping in to challenge racists both during and after
incidents (including via formal complaints), as in the following report about security
guards policing a shopping centre area.

       Around 1 pm today … I saw two First Nations women in the carpark area of the
       [named] Shopping Centre … I had seen them in the area before, and the previous
       day they were sitting in a park … while I was getting lunch. They are kind, very
       friendly women. I planned to do some shopping at the vegetable shop and return
       to give them some change on the way back to my car. However, as I walked out of
       the shop, I saw a young, female security guard … screaming at the women. I
       stopped to listen and heard her tell them they are not allowed in the shopping
       precinct area and if they did not leave, she would call police. The women politely
       replied that they were not doing anything wrong but they would leave regardless
       …. I told her that if she did not leave the women alone immediately, I would be
       reporting her racist, discriminatory, and abusive actions. She told me that she
       was just doing her job. I returned to my car and as I was driving through the
       carpark, I saw the security officer had been joined by another female security
       officer …. They were yelling and intimidating the women, following them as they
       headed off the premises … I told both security guards that I would be reporting
       them for discrimination and verbal abuse. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

In response to harassment by a neighbour, potentially causing a First Nations woman to
leave public housing, the friend/relative reporting the incident states that ‘With Aunt's
permission I spoke to [the] neighbour saying that her behaviour is against the law and I
will call the police if it continues’ (friend/relative report, non-Indigenous). Note that only
1% had reported incidents to police (3% of self-reports) – unsurprising given issues of
trust and racism within policing raised in other parts of this report (Table 30, Appendix A).

Most commonly, people talked to family and friends following racism (21%, see Figure
19). The First Nations man who experienced racism in conversation with his non-
Indigenous in-laws identified this as a positive response.

       I felt worthless until I talked to my father and he said I did the right thing by kicking
       them out of my home. He said you not only did it for yourself. You did it for me for



                                              75
       your auntie and uncles your grandparents and your future children. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal male)

Examples of ‘other type of report or complaint’ or ‘other action’ (15% and 8%
respectively, see Figure 19) include the action taken by witnesses to racism perpetrated
by the comedian discussed earlier. ‘I wrote to the venue requesting they make a public
denouncement of her and reassure the wider community that this would never happen
again’ (witness report, non-Indigenous). The First Nations employee concerned about a
racist student nurse took the following action.

       As it was my first day at this job and this person already had connections with my
       coworkers, I felt uncomfortable confronting her about this. I have reported the
       interaction to her University though as I don't believe this person should be
       working within regional healthcare with her attitude. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

A range of strategies was employed by the First Nations academic reporting racism
experienced at the hands of a student, including taking internal and external legal and
other action.

       … reported to my boss, asked student to leave the classroom the second time it
       happened, reported to university support service, told my Dean, told my PVC
       Indigenous, told colleagues I trusted, told my [named Union] branch president,
       increased therapy frequency, hired a lawyer when the union proved useless. (Self-
       report, Aboriginal female)

Other actions reported included working for a First Nations legal organisation offering
support to First Nations people in the face of discriminatory drinking laws in the NT
(friend/relative report, non-Indigenous) and as identified by multiple people, use of the
Call It Out Register.

       I have waited for the heat to subside. I want this incident recorded somewhere
       that sees it counted as racism against Aboriginal people. I am still weighing
       whether it reaches the threshold for a complaint to the Ombudsman, though I am
       adding it to my existing file of evidence with them. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

       As I was frustrated and angry... I vented to a colleague who is Aboriginal-identified
       and she referred me to make this complaint. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

       Today I felt the only action I could manage was this one - to call it out [on this
       Register]. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

There are also multiple accounts shared throughout this report indicating that
disengaging, avoiding the place/person and not saying or doing anything in response to
racism is not uncommon (in combination, 23% of reports) (see Figure 19). We consider
the very significant barriers inhibiting responses to racism in [3.3].

                                            76
Avoidance is evident, for instance, where First Nations people leave a job or stay away
from the place in which racism has occurred. ‘I actually haven't caught a tram since the
incident! I've gone back onto my anxiety medication since the incident happened’ (self-
report, Aboriginal female). ‘I won't be using that store ever again’ (self-report, Aboriginal
female). Avoidance or disengagement may be responses that sit alongside others
(including defending oneself/others). And we note too that these are not necessarily
unconstructive responses to racism, as identified in previous Call It Out reports. They
can be a form of self-preservation, as the following reports related to social media
incidents suggest.

       Didn't want to give oxygen to this person and their views, so just blocked and
       deleted them. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

       Facebook profile … really got to me this morning and triggered my own racist
       experiences. I can't understand or accept why his profile is getting away with
       posting such racist statements and memes. This may seem trivial, but today I'm
       not having it! I don't want to waste my energy focusing on [this individual’s]
       personal racism, because it makes me physically sick, annoyed, distraught and
       I'm no longer being quiet about racism! I'm over it all, my frustrations at people
       who are unable to feel empathy, compassion and being non-judgemental is only
       growing every day. It's so sad that people are still thinking like this in 2024! (Self-
       report, Aboriginal)

At other times, these types of responses look more like exclusion, shunning, isolation or
similarly negative outcomes (see also discussion of disengagement from school in [4]).
For instance, when a manager refused to allow a First Nations employee to ‘set the team
budget even though other’ non-Aboriginal staff at similar levels ‘had full autonomy over
their team budgets’ this employee resigned from their role, ‘leading to loss of income’
(self-report, Aboriginal female).

3.2.2 Responses to the incident for those who self-reported racism, by gender

We have also investigated responses to incidents of racism by gender for those who self-
reported racism. Of this group, more than half (80/155 or 52%) chose to respond to this
optional question, and a majority of these (54/85 or 68%) selected multiple responses
(n=170, see Table 32 in Appendix A). As above, in 2024-25 respondents could select up
to a maximum of three responses for this question.

‘Talked to family or friends’ was the most frequent response for both genders (26%
females and 24% males) (see also Table 32 in Appendix A), as was the case in our
previous two annual reports for 2022-23 and 2023-24.

Although the numbers are small, males were proportionately more likely to ‘disengage’
(14% males compared to 9% females). While females were more likely to report directly


                                             77
to the organisation/service or internal HR (13% females compared to 8% males). Males
were proportionately more likely to make a complaint to an independent complaints
body (10% males compared to 3% females) and slightly more likely to report to police
(5% males compared to 3% females). Both genders were equally likely to retaliate (both
3%) (See Table 32 in Appendix A). 45

3.3        Barriers to calling out racism

As noted above, a sizeable number of persons identify disengaging, avoiding a
place/person or doing or saying nothing when encountering racism. This speaks to the
enormous challenge of calling racism out.

Individuals completing the Register
were asked to identify up to three
main barriers to responding to
racism from a choice of 12 answers.
This was a new question on the
Register in 2024-25, and more than
half (261/442 or 59%) of those filling
in the Register completed this
optional question. Of these, more
than half (203/261 or 78%) provided
multiple responses (n=621, see
Table 33 in Appendix A).

As shown in Figure 20, ‘lack of trust in
the system’ was the most common
barrier to calling out racism (15%),
including for each respondent group
(see Table 33 in Appendix A). Other
barriers more frequently identified,
as shown in Figure 20, include
‘reported before and nothing

There were some differences in barriers for different groups reporting to the Register (see
detail at Table 33 in Appendix A),46 and across targeted age groups. For instance, for
reported incidents of racism targeting children and young people in the 0-19 age group,
the most common barrier identified was ‘don’t trust the system’ (19%), while ‘fear of job
loss’ was somewhat more likely for incidents targeting adults in the 30-39 age group
(11%) (Table 34 in Appendix A).

3.3.1 Nothing to be done about racism

The barriers identified as ‘not worth it nothing ever changes’, ‘reported before and
nothing happened’ and to an extent, ‘don’t trust the system’ all speak to similar issues
and collectively make up a sizeable 38% of all responses (Figure 20). They are
interconnected issues, at certain points. Lack of trust arises, for instance, where ‘the
system’ fails to respond appropriately to racism. This system could be an HR or other
internal system through which an employee might seek a remedy, legal system
protections against racism or perhaps how the mainstream world operates more broadly
(and however else this term is interpreted by those responding to this question). There
was, understandably, an overarching sense that people can still get away with racism
and that there was very little to be done about it.

        There is no recourse for these acts of racism. Our society allows it. They are
        entitled to act this way and if we respond we are the problem. (Friend/Relative
        report, Aboriginal)

As previously discussed, there are variable and unpredictable outcomes of calling out
racism. Multiple accounts shared to the Register and throughout this report identify poor
responses to challenges to racism – whether that be via formal complaints mechanisms
or when defending oneself/others directly (in conversation with a racist, for example). As
a further example, the academic who experienced racism from a student identified other
students as ‘great allies in checking in with me after class to see if I was ok and praised
my handling of the matter’ (self-report, Aboriginal female). The university’s response was
identified as falling short, however – as discussed earlier.

        I expected the student to be removed from my subject but university support
        services that investigated did not recognise any racism and took 3 months to
        investigate so student stayed in my subject but as an online student and got to

compared to reports from friends/relatives (3%) and First Nations people directly experiencing racism
(9%). See further detail at Table 33, Appendix A.

       failing, only written assessments count. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

The First Nations family member reporting harassment by a church congregation
member ‘approached the leadership team’ ‘with no result other than that: “We need to
understand age. This lady is old and will never change”’ (self-report, Aboriginal female).
As was recorded in previous Call It Out reports, those failing to moderate content online
are also identified as racist. ‘Meta is terrible at mitigating racism’ (witness report, non-
Indigenous).

       This page [on social media] contains videos calling for violence towards
       Aboriginal First Nations [people] in [named town] etc. The comments prove this. I
       have reported this page to Facebook with no success. This is 1 of a number of
       pages. (Self-report, Aboriginal)

Lodging complaints with anti-discrimination bodies or other independent complaints
body was not especially common as a response to racism (4%, Figure 19) but for one
First Nations person who did so the body in question ‘weren't even sure how to support’
(self-report, Aboriginal female).

In terms of challenges to racism being ‘not worth it, nothing ever changes’ (10%, Figure
20), people questioned the ‘time it takes’ and ‘whether it actually affects change’,
including where incidents or issues are more ‘systemic’ in nature. (Witness report, non-
Indigenous). Also discussed is that the power to bring about change sits with those that
are likely to be part of the problem. This was noted in discussing challenges in reporting
the Church Dean to the senior Bishop (see [2.2]). Another relevant comment is as
follows.

       It's enormous. And very long standing. And serves [the] interests of the powerful
       who actually have capacity to change things. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Those using the Register felt that there was not enough proof or evidence to do anything
about racism (9%, Figure 20). That First Nations people might know they are being
discriminated against, but face difficulties proving this is illustrated in the following
reports. These describe First Nations people calling out racism ‘in the moment’ - when
subjected to over-surveillance in stores (see also [2.4.2]). Attempts to identify racism
may (apparently relatively easily) be countered with ‘well, where is the evidence?’.

       I said is this pick on black people day. The female said you’re the second person
       who said that and it's not because of the colour of your skin. I asked why are you
       not stopping … white people that were leaving the store. This was racial profiling
       and unconscious bias towards me and I felt it and knew it was and I called it out.
       Unacceptable behaviour. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)




                                            80
       Walked into the store with my father, we both have a dark complexion and the
       worker used her earpiece walkie talkie to tell the other worker out loud to watch
       me and my father after we were going to get engine coolant. As soon as we got our
       item the worker quickly radioed the other colleague don't worry and played it off
       as a joke when it was a clear that she was racially profiling us when other non-
       Indigenous customers that walked ahead of us were not told to be watched. (Self-
       report, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander female)

This last report continues as follows.

       … Made me realise that racial profiling is still happening in this day and age. I
       imagined the days of going into a shop without being the target of racism were less
       prevalent and more subtle. Understanding that Australia has a subtle subculture
       of treating Indigenous people differently to white people. (Self-report, Aboriginal
       and Torres Strait Islander female)

A fear of ‘job loss/other career impacts’, ‘other negative consequences’ or ‘backlash’ of
some description constituted 19% (combined, Figure 20). The witness who reported a
customer speaking of running over an Aboriginal person did not respond at the time due
to fear, for example.

       I had to continue serving them due to a fear of potential escalation. I had to advise
       the team manager of what happened and he was not reassuring as he mentioned
       it is unlikely they are able to do anything to do anything. (Witness report,
       Aboriginal)

An Aboriginal woman who reported being told to ‘move over you black cunts’ by a
stranger on the street also didn’t challenge this individual, stating ‘I'm scared of getting
stabbed’ (self-report, Aboriginal female). And certainly, as we have seen, calling out
racism can and does have real-life and weighty negative consequences (for example, the
Aboriginal woman arrested when videoing a young person’s assault in a store). The
following report discusses fear of repercussions arising in a workplace setting.

       Prior to us meeting [an Aboriginal organisation] my manager presented her
       concerns about attending the meeting [with this organisation] as the only white
       person and said, "so do I need to be careful as they might spear me with their
       spears". She laughed but stopped once she seen my facial expressions become
       very uncomfortable and how my tone was when I said that's a racist thing to say,
       how dare you. I only started in the role 2 weeks prior and felt isolated as … I didn't
       want to get into a conflict that could see me losing this new opportunity in an
       instant that I worked very hard to achieve. I've been in this situation many times
       and when I have called it out I was shone upon and people stayed clear of me for
       worry of their mouths saying the wrong things about my people. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal)


                                            81
Related to this, intimidation was seen as a tactic purposefully used to silence challenges
to racism – in this instance in online spaces.

       This [named social media account] keeps trying to intimate me by saying his
       admins are from VIC Pol[ice] and WA Pol[ice] and are looking into my place of
       employment. And that's illegal as I know the law very well. I have also reported
       these posts, and Facebook has done nothing among more and more comments.
       (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

‘Social emotional wellbeing/health’ barriers inhibiting responses (7%, Figure 20) might
include the above-mentioned fear, as well as other issues. It may be just too
overwhelming in general (wellbeing wise) to take on racism.

       They accuse the victim of being the perpetrator and isn't taken seriously. Also
       constantly repeating the story is re-traumatising. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

For this reason, people may choose (or as follows, be encouraged) to avoid taking action
as a form of self-protection – unless absolutely necessary. This may link with a further
barrier identified; that an issue or incident may not be seen as ‘serious enough’ to
warrant taking action (7%, Figure 20).

       I have had management (even Aboriginal management) tell me to leave it before.
       Pick my battles, separate myself from the ones who are angry. But I feel angry too.
       (Self-report, Aboriginal)

For this same First Nations person, not taking action in this instance made them ‘feel like
I'm betraying’ grandchildren (who are also likely to face racism in future – pointing to the
intergenerational nature of racism).

The barrier related to the costs (6%, Figure 20) may relate to financial but perhaps also
other (for example, emotional) costs associated with taking action. One Aboriginal
female reported that they ‘Tried to gain a no win no fee lawyer … and they refused to take
it on’ (self-report, Aboriginal female). One witness raised lack of knowledge/clarity about
legalities associated with racist online content as somehow ‘permitting’ such behaviour.
This includes legalities about what content is or isn’t against the law and who has
responsibility (legally) when such content is shared – and somewhat related to this point
is the barrier of ‘not being sure what to do or say’ (11%, Figure 20). Below we also discuss
the murkiness of laws when students post social media content outside of school.

       Gross online posts and comments by many in my community about [young
       people] throwing rocks at cars in my community. Understand community anger -
       but lots of ‘bashing until teeth fall out’ kind of responses. Some jumping in to call
       it out but with all the aggression, it's intimidating to do so … These people have no
       shame and think they will have no accountability. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)


                                            82
3.3.2 Barriers to calling out racism for those who self-reported racism, by gender

We also investigated barriers to standing up to racism by gender for those who self-
reported racism. Of this group, just under half (76/155 or 49%) selected to respond to
this question, and a majority of these (66/76 or 87%) selected multiple responses (n=200,
see Table 35 in Appendix A). As above, respondents could select up to three responses
for this optional question.

Females were more proportionately more likely to report not trusting the system (17%
females and 9% males), fear of job loss or career impacts (10% females and 6% males)
and social/emotional wellbeing or health reasons (9% females and 3% males) (Table 35,
Appendix A).

Males were more likely to identify lack of proof/evidence (males 13% and females 6%),
cost of making a complaint (males 13% and females 6%) and not sure what to do or say
(13% males compared to 10% females) (Table 35, Appendix A).

3.4     What needs to be done to combat racism

The Register also contained a question on what needs to be done to combat racism. In
2024-25, a maximum of three responses could be nominated for this question.47 More
than half of all respondents (280/442 or 63%) completed this optional question, and
most of those people (255/280 or 91%) provided multiple responses (n=779, see Table
36 in Appendix A).

As shown in Figure 21 below, the most frequently identified solution for combatting
racism was ‘First Nations Sovereignty (e.g. self-determination, land back, reparations)’
and ‘increase everyone’s understanding about First Nations culture and history’ (both
14%) (see also Table 36 in Appendix A). This strategy, in combination with the third most
common response, ‘stronger legal protections against and penalties for racism’
accounted for over a third of all responses (40%) (see Table 36 in Appendix A).

These were the most common solutions identified for self-reports and witness reports.
However, for friend/relative reports the most common solutions were ‘educate the
community on how to stand up against racism’ (16%), followed by ‘stronger legal
protections against and penalties for racism’ (14%) and ‘increase public awareness
about racism and its impacts on First Nations people’ (12%). (See Table 36 in Appendix
A).




47
  In previous years there was no restriction on the number of ndividual responses for this question. As a
result, there was little differentiation between answers identified in previous annual reports. A limit of up
to 3 answers was introduced in 2024-25 to better understand key solutions for combatting racism
identified by those who reported experiencing and witnessing racism.

                                                     83

was the most common solution in reports where the person being targeted was identified

were equally likely to identify ‘increased education and public awareness campaigns to

3.4.1 What needs to be done to combat racism for those who self-reported racism,

We analysed responses to the question of what needs to be done to combat racism by
gender for those who self-reported racism. Of this group, just under half (76/155 or 49%)
chose to respond to this question, and of these a majority (71/76 or 93%) selected
multiple responses (n=217, see Table 37 in Appendix A). As above, in 2024-25
respondents could select up to a maximum of three answers for this optional question.


                                           84
First Nations Sovereignty was a common response to the question of what needs to be
done to combat racism by gender of those who self-reported experiencing racism. There
was little (1 percentage point) differentiation between responses for males (14%) and
females (13%). (Table 33, Appendix A).

There were some notable differences in other responses by gender, however the
numbers are relatively small. Taken together males were more likely to identify other First
Nations self-determination and governance strategies 48 by a difference of 18 percentage
points (52% males compared to 34% females). Males were more likely to identify
stronger legal protections against and penalties for racism (16% males compared to 12%
females), giving more First Nations peoples a voice on this issue (16% males and 11%

Taken together, education and awareness related strategies targeting the broader
community/society49 were more frequently identified by females (43%) than males
(25%); except for responses identifying ‘educate the community on how to stand up
against racism’ which were similar (9% females and 10% males). (Table 37, Appendix A).

3.4.2 Strategies to combat racism

We heard that multiple different approaches and strategies are required to tackle racism,
given its enormity and complexity. ‘Anti-racism is the work of everyone. This needs to be
embedded culturally, politically, legally’ (friend/relative report, non-Indigenous). This
probably accounts for the similarity in preferred responses to racism, as above (see
Figure 20). As one First Nations woman stated in response to this question, ‘It won't let
me select 'all of the above' but ALL OF THE ABOVE. It ALL needs to happen’ (self-report,
Aboriginal female).

Rights and responsibilities
That everyone should be combatting racism came through in various reports, including
those speaking of the reluctance of some to take on this responsibility. Others were

       It's powerless [to call it out directly] without the right platforms that hold racists

Enhanced legal protections against racism accounted for a relatively high 25% of all
responses when combining the following strategies: ‘stronger legal protections against
and penalties for racism’ (12%), ‘educate the public about the legal and ethical
responsibilities of being anti-racist’ (5%), ‘more accessible and safer complaints
processes for reporting racism’ (5%) and ‘increase First Nations awareness about how
to use the law to challenge racism’ (3%) (see Figure 21).

As this data indicates, responses were somewhat less centred on initiation of
complaints or legal action, including by First Nations people (8%, combining better
complaints mechanisms and First Nations awareness of how to use the law), compared
with measures for increasing accountability of others to avoid or address racism (17%,
combining having stronger protections in place and increased awareness about
responsibilities to avoid breaching them) (see Figure 21). This perhaps speaks to the
important role of the law in changing behaviours proactively and preventatively as an
alternative to placing the onus on those impacted by racism to take legal action. There
are significant barriers for First Nations people affected by racism to challenge it via the
legal system, some of which are touched on above (for example, costs, distrust).

(Stronger) legal provisions as solutions to racism include but extend beyond human
rights law. One First Nations person called for stronger ‘social media laws to protect

against unauthorized videos and racist intent’, for instance.50 Other comments include
the following.

           … I despair for Aboriginal people being inflicted [with] this daily abuse - this abuse
           has grown stronger since the failed Referendum- these people feel … safety [in]
           numbers to be openly racist. I feel Australia needs a human rights charter.
           Something needs to happen. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

           Prosecute perpetrators. Make examples of their behaviours and sanction
           them...!!! (Witness report, Aboriginal)

           Policies and stronger laws with consequences supported by a massive PR push
           to the community and in all media showing and highlighting bad behaviours. They
           must be legislated as permanent prime time short grabs in all [mainstream

           Large fines and demotion for racial microaggressions. Loss of Blue card and
           Yellow Card and ability to work with vulnerable people. Racial molesting is trauma
           and mental health and lifespan eroding. Prison time for racial crimes. (Witness
           report, not identified)

While referring to the fishing competition interview, one First Nations man identified
Articles 15 and 16 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
(UNDRIP) as provding essential legal protection against racism (witness report,
Aboriginal). We cite these provisions in full here, as they were in the report.51

     Article 15, UNDRIP
     1. Indigenous peoples have the right to the dignity and diversity of their cultures, traditions,
     histories and aspirations which shall be appropriately reflected in education and public
     information.
     2. States shall take effective measures, in consultation and cooperation with the Indigenous
     peoples concerned, to combat prejudice and eliminate discrimination and to promote
     tolerance, understanding and good relations among Indigenous peoples and all other
     segments of society.
     Article 16, UNDRIP
     1. Indigenous peoples have the right to establish their own media in their own languages and
     to have access to all forms of non-Indigenous media without discrimination.
     2. States shall take effective measures to ensure that State-owned media duly reflect
     Indigenous cultural diversity. States, without prejudice to ensuring full freedom of
     expression, should encourage privately-owned media to adequately reflect Indigenous
     cultural diversity.

Understanding and attitudes

The following report identifies ‘training’ as necessary to lift government accountability to
address racism – part of a broader common theme of working on understanding and
attitudes to combat this issue.

       The local council needs independent oversight and training to improve their
       servicing. The racist divide is tangible and disgusting. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

Public education and awareness strategies together accounted for 39% of responses,
combining the following strategies: ‘increase everyone’s understanding about First
Nations culture and history’ (14%), ‘educate the community on how to stand up against
racism’ (10%), ‘increase public awareness about racism and its impact on First Nations
people’ (7%), ‘educate the public about the legal/ethical responsibilities to be anti-
racist’ (5%) and ‘increase First Nations awareness about how to use the law to challenge
racism’ (3%) (see Figure 21). Various reports spoke of these strategies, including as
follows.

       I think white Australians on the coast haven't been even introduced to a wide
       variety of Indigenous peoples so they believe a stereotype they've been taught by
       their parents is what Indigenous people are. As well as that white Australians on
       the coast don't care that Indigenous peoples were first on land and should be
       respected. I think people who are not of Aboriginal descent need to be educated
       that Indigenous Australians need to be respected and treated the same as them,
       because there is still a big racial inequity. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       [A racist incident on social media] made me realise that many non-Indigenous
       Australians have extremely superficial knowledge and understanding of
       Indigenous cultures. It makes you lose faith in people and society. (Witness
       report, non-Indigenous)

One witness to an incident involving denigration of a prominent First Nations athlete
emphasised this point.

       The incident has motivated me to research more into Aboriginal athletes in the
       sporting world and the accomplishments they have achieved. It has made me
       eager to learn more about how Australia is supporting First Nations athletes and
       this way, I can then be better informed when perpetrators of racism do make
       discriminatory statements. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Changing attitudes is identified as crucial. We note that racist attitudes and stereotypes
are consistently the most commonly reported type of racism identified in our annual
reports.



                                            88
       … I felt disheartened about how many people were so comfortable and confident
       perpetuating harmful stereotypes about Aboriginal people. It reflects that there is
       a still long way to go to change social attitudes towards Aboriginal people.
       (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Increased understanding of culture and history may address some of the ignorant and
harmful racism reported to the Register, including where these incidents demonstrate
poor recognition of culture, for instance. This might perhaps help increase society’s
empathic and ‘trauma based responses’; essential due to our ‘colonial history’ (self-
report, Aboriginal male). Increasing empathy was identified in a report about a recent
trend involving use of a First Nations man’s image when making video-calls (for some
reason, seen as humorous).

       [The incident] left me feeling frustrated that people did not take the time to think
       about the harm they are perpetuating. I wish they had taken a moment to think
       about how they would feel if someone from their own family was used by
       complete strangers for something like this. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Others suggested that increasing empathy (or changing attitudes generally) would be
impossible and as such, mechanisms of accountability are (also) certainly required – in
this instance, a name and shame register (suggested in previous Call It Out reporting).
This again highlights the importance of multi-layered strategies.

       If I could, I would tick all of these. There is one problem (apart from the limit [to
       number of options to select]). People like this will never be convinced by listening
       to the experiences of others. There is an ingrained narcissism that resents being
       asked to reflect and place oneself in the shoes of another. In many ways we
       almost need a name-and-shame register: this seems to be the only thing that's
       likely to shift attitudes with these people. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Education is also identified as occurring in less formal settings; where individuals step
up, speak up and act as good role models, including for younger generations. There are
different ways to build understanding, it is suggested, which don’t always have to be
directly centred on teaching people about avoiding being racist.

       Knowing that the solution does not sit with reporting it, more so with adults being
       good role models and providing education from a young age. (Witness report, non-
       Indigenous)

       I thought "respecting the difference" would help. Now I teach nurses, midwives
       and doctors about First Nations health and wellbeing. Change is going to be slow
       and frankly painful. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)




                                            89
Strength in culture and self-determination

As noted, preferred strategies incorporate and centre First Nations self-determination
(through First Nations Sovereignty, amplifying First Nations voices and prioritising First
Nations-led responses and solutions (33% in combination, Figure 21)). First Nations
people are already taking action to combat racism, as we have seen throughout this
report - and as the following report by a friend/relative identifies.

       Sitting running a workshop about justice system with Aboriginal people for work.
       Every Aboriginal participant had been locked up or had family currently locked up.
       Shameful situation we are in in this country. Very stark reminder of the shit that
       happens on a daily basis to our First Nations peoples but inspired by their resolve
       at that workshop to take action to bring about change. (Friend/Relative report,
       non-Indigenous)

This may also, in part, involving talking to friends/family when experiencing racism, the
most commonly identified response to incidents. Strong Indigenous leadership was
highlighted too as a key solution, as was strengthening of culture.

       Build stronger communities and individuals, to stop following the way of life we
       lived on missions and communities, be loving leaders in their families, pick up the
       value of Kinship relationships, extra mothers and fathers, extra Grandmothers
       and Grandfathers, find language words for those people - drop the false name
       words Aunty, Uncle, cousins we have our own language words find them and use
       them… Relearn our culture … organise camps in our own lands, find our own
       designs, check museums to see if they have items that represent certain cultural
       property you belong to. Be true to ourselves, teach our kids. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)




                                           90
4. Children and young people
The focus in this section of the Report is on incidents of racism impacting children and
young people (0-19 age group). This is a focus given the increase this year in reports about
and from this age group - and for this reason, we have included as an introductory piece
thoughts from a young First Nations woman about racism and her responses to it.

Reports to the Register impact this group in different ways. Sometimes incidents are
reported by adults where younger people are the direct targets of racism. In other adult-
initiated reports, this group is less directly targeted but are still impacted. The latter might
include, for example, when incidents target their parents or other First Nations people,
such as social media incidents.

Younger people might also report incidents themselves – most likely where they are
directly targeted. One example of this is a comment shared to the Register by a young
Aboriginal person describing racism as experienced constantly and viscerally.

        Everywhere I go no matter where, if it's around non-Indigenous people I feel a hate
        vibe. It feels like I'm being watched. (Self-Report, Aboriginal)

Adults reporting to the Register may also identify incidents that occurred in their youth,
with significant and lasting impacts. Or in some cases the whole family can be directly
targeted, as occurred in the report concerning the church congregation member.
Incidents that fit into each of these categories are shared throughout the report and
discussed in more detail below, along with responses to such incidents and their
impacts.

4.1     Racism experienced by children and young people

We recorded at [2.7.2] that more than a quarter of those who identified the age of the
victim of incidents selected the 0-19 years age group.52 Thus, a significant proportion of
reports, where age was known, impacted children and young people.

‘Negative or ignorant attitudes or stereotyping’ and ‘verbal abuse or hate speech’ were
proportionately more prevalent as types of racism for all age groups, including those
aged 0-19. However, those aged 0-19 were more likely than other age groups to
experience bullying/threats/intimidation and physical harm (see Table 21 in Appendix A).

Perhaps not surprisingly, those aged 0-19 were also likely to have experienced racism in
a school/educational setting (30% of identified locations of racism). Other media and
social media/online were also frequent locations (16% and 15% respectively) (Figure A).

      The fellow student went around telling other students in my year group saying, "I

Incidents were reported by First Nations adults recounting experiences of racism as a
student at school – and again, involving student perpetrators. The below report and
others set out in this section identify racist hate speech and verbal abuse.

      I used to go to a predominantly Pacific Islander high school. I was moved there in
      hopes of a fresh new start because my last high school wasn't the best for me.
      Everyone there was always asking me what I was ethnically, obviously because I
      was the new girl. Of course, I answered with "I'm Aboriginal & Tongan". They all
      knew I was half Aboriginal. Yet all they would do was throw the word "abo" around
      and be racist right in front of me... There was this girl who'd always say horrible
      things about Blakfullas then would look at me, laugh, and say "oh I wasn't talking
      to you, don't worry". But I knew she was. Another time I was walking to class and
      that same girl screamed out "ABO" to this other Blak boy. I felt horrible for him.
      There was only about 5 Blakfullas there including me … Another time, someone
      was talking about a bad incident in class and I happened to overhear it.
      Apparently, the perpetrator was Aboriginal. Then some guy said, "bloody abos."
      As if we're some kind of disgusting group of people who all condone and do that
      stuff... that's the first time I've ever heard of something like that happen. All ethnic
      groups across the world [have their] good and bad … (Self-report, Aboriginal
      female)

Other incidents of racism at school were reported by friends and parents of children
targeted.

       My friends were walking around school & other students called them "ab*s" whilst
       pointing at them. (Friend/Relative report, non-Indigenous)

       My daughter was called coon by one of her peers. They were taking the piss out of
       each other, he called her ugly, so she called him Pugsley and he responded with
       well you're a coon. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

       My daughter is in year six at Primary School. The incident occurred during a
       lesson. The class was studying history and Aboriginal culture in particular when
       there were derogatory comments made by another child in the classroom. The
       class was watching a video on a corroboree when this child said it sounds like his
       parents when they are drunk at 3am. At another point during the lesson this same
       child referred to Aboriginal people as violent. At another point during the writing
       session that followed the same child asked the teacher for the name of the toy
       monkey with cymbals. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

Incidents also involved school staff. For instance, the last report above goes on to state
that the teacher did not respond to the comments by the year six student.

       My daughter was very upset about the comments. Unfortunately, the teacher did
       not address any of the comments. It is uncertain if the teacher heard the first two
       comments, but my daughter was able to hear them and she was not at the same
       table as the child making these comments. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

Other incidents recounted individual staff directly perpetrating racism, not just failing to
respond to it.

       It was while the yes, no Referendum was going on in 2023. It came up [as a] topic
       in class at school and the whole class including the teacher goes on saying why
       we don't deserve it etc. I was left feeling targeted. (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       I was attending music class where the teacher referred to the blues music and its
       basis in slavery as "nigger music". (Self-report, Aboriginal, non-binary)

       Teacher of mental health refuses to do Acknowledgement of Country and tried to
       minimise the experiences of people and families that are a part of the Stolen
       Generation. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

       My 10 year old was told to write a narrative from the perspective of Captain Cook.
       When he raised [that] this was racist (alongside the other information the
       students are being taught about so called discovery and settlement of Australia),
       he was told this is your opinion. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)



                                            94
As noted previously, incidents perpetrated by individuals constitutes institutional racism
where it demonstrates patterns of behaviour and/or where racism is poorly addressed by
institutions or organisations. The failure by schools to respond to racism appropriately
was called out in a number of reports.

       Child in grade 4 called another child a 'N____R' and the teacher heard it and did
       nothing. Victim then hit perpetrator and got in trouble. School wants each child to
       apologise to each other. End of story they said. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

       An Aboriginal friend told me about how her child has been called racist names at
       school multiple times. Despite multiple complaints the school were yet to do
       anything effective about it. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

The student whose music teacher used the ‘N__’ word in class also identifies a poor
response to a complaint she lodged about the incident.

       … I reported her for it making sure my identity as an Aboriginal was known
       specifically because everyone in the class was white or white passing and I
       wanted to put an emphasis on the harm that she's committing specifically when
       she thinks only white people are around. I was then subjected to a harassment
       campaign by her, her friends who were my other teachers and school faculty until
       I decided to drop her class, classes her friends taught, and eventually had to leave
       school entirely. The school said all they could do about it was make her apologise
       and they wouldn't do anything further. They also tried to act like forcing me to drop
       her class instead of punishing the racist was doing me a favour. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal, non-binary)

The parent who reported racism in a year 6 classroom described escalating a complaint
– again, without a satisfactory outcome. This report identifies failure on the part of the
school to take racism sufficiently seriously at a policy and practical level.

       I called the school that same day and asked to speak to the principal and teacher.
       I told the school that my child was very upset and did not want to return to the
       classroom, particularly since they were doing a series of lessons on Australian
       history and the racism was likely to continue. The principal called me back the
       next day at lunch time, which demonstrated a lack of concern about the matter. I
       asked to meet with the principal as a matter of urgency on the issue to discuss an
       anti-racism procedure for the school. The principal has confirmed that she cannot
       meet me for a week as she has meetings. She also said that of course the school
       has a policy on racism but did not know it offhand. The principal also said that she
       is really the middle person, between the teacher and the parent. I told the
       principal that I was happy to talk to the teacher but was reporting the racism
       higher up as it falls within the principal’s remit. The principal was entirely



                                            95
       unconcerned with the issue and was aware that my child did not want to return to
       her classroom as she felt unsafe. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

A similar account was shared to the Register by a witness.

       A young Indigenous 12 year old girl has been racially bullied at an eastern
       Victorian secondary school. She has been racially abused by multiple students
       including peers and friends. It has been a repeated cycle because she has
       reported it to the school who then only asks the offending student to write a letter
       of apology to the girl directly and is suspended. She has felt embarrassed and
       upset about her Indigenous heritage due to this. The racism has since stopped for
       approximately 3 weeks but she fears it may continue and that apologies are not
       enough to change people's racist behaviour and own internal racist thoughts.
       (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

4.3    Other racism targeting children and young people

Social media/media related reports sometimes crossed over with school-based
incidents. A report was made by a First Nations parent whose son saw an image online,
which was content created by students at his school. The image depicted two girls: one
in full Black-Face holding a sign that says ‘I’m a <N> prostitute’ (with the word fully
spelled out); the other holding a sign that says ‘I am Suicide Night’ (with love hearts
around it). We describe below at [4.5] what happened when this was reported to the
school.

Another report identified a very ‘light touch’ response by a private school in the wake of
racist social media posted by its students.

       ABC News report: An elite private school in WA, '[names school] received a
       complaint about the messages sent over the social media app Snapchat, then
       screenshots were circulated within the school community. The school became
       aware of the messages and due to its position as private independent institutions,
       was not required to notify the Department of Education or the WA minister for
       education. The ABC has chosen not to show the messages as they contain
       offensive depictions of Indigenous people. The messages contained racial slurs
       against Indigenous Australians, including references to suicide, sexual abuse,
       and alcohol use... [named school principal] told the ABC the school did not
       comment on student matters. "[Named school] is committed to fostering an
       inclusive, respectful learning environment for all students, from pre-kindergarten




                                            96
        to year 12," she said. "We value diversity and the importance of learning from one
        another in a supportive way."58 (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

Social media/media related incidents involving victims aged 0-19 frequently cross over
with criminal legal system related issues and stereotyping too. For example, the raising
of past offending in the interview with the fishing competition winner (aged 19 at the
time), which as noted, leant and fed into common stereotypes of First Nations young
people as ‘law breakers’. Other social media incidents reported similar stereotyping, as
well as aggressive racism (threats of harm) that directly targeted First Nations young
people alleged to have committed a crime.

        Local [named town] community group using skin colour as the only descriptor of
        a 5 year old child they claim was attempting to steal a bike. Almost all [online]
        comments were blaming drug and alcohol addicted parents. Many suggesting
        that they would use a bat to discipline the 5 year old child. Others were writing the
        entire child's future off. Lots of grouping language such as they're all like this and
        other very thinly veiled racist remarks. Reported to group admins and no action
        was taken. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

        A person posted on the [named town] noticeboard a video of some youth breaking
        into a sushi shop. Two people commented and talked about how they could
        sniper them and shoot them. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

As the above illustrates, discussion online of alleged offending by young people can lead
to (mass) racist commentary related to First Nations people in general. The following
report from a First Nations person aged 0-19 included multiple screenshots of such
commentary (see below).

        I am a member of a Facebook neighbourhood page for [named town]. There has
        been a photo put up of a group of young Aboriginal boys, one of them threw food
        at someone's car. This person has uploaded the images to Facebook and there
        has been a spill of violent and hate speech about the boys. Threats to run the boy
        over, and use of discriminatory words and descriptions about Aboriginal people. I
        have reported it a few times and nothing has happened. (Witness report,
        Aboriginal)

In discussion of the criminal legal system ([2.4.4]) and law, policy and practice ([2.3.3])
criminal law was identified as disproportionately impacting young First Nations people,
with specific reference to bail laws and racial profiling by police.

As a specific example, over-policing with intrusive surveillance was reported by non-
Indigenous witnesses concerned about increased deployment of night cameras in a
local area, directly linked to the surveillance of First Nations children. Concerns were
raised that young people were being criminalised and that children would be more fearful
of police as a result. The witness reporting this incident addresses the broader
implications for trust and wellbeing and the racialised nature of police surveillance
towards First Nations children in the local community.

       Recently police have increased their surveillance of the youth, many of whom are
       First Nations children. They have set up night cameras and increased police
       presence. These kinds of tactics lead to the kids being more fearful and disdainful
       of police and police in turn being more likely to criminalise the kids. (Witness
       report, non-Indigenous)

As noted in [4.1], physical harm was proportionately more frequently reported as a type
of racism experienced by children/young people.60 Examples of this outside of policing
include the following incident occurring in a public space.

        While walking along the road in the streets of [named town, QLD] it wasn't unusual
        for a car to swerve at you and scream racial slurs out the car. There was this one
        time that has stuck with me when 3 of my mates and myself were waking back
        from a school function and a white car swerved at us almost colliding and
        screaming "you filthy blacks". Luckily, we were aware of our area and was able to
        move quick away from the situation and run up a different street. (Self-report,
        Aboriginal male)

One deeply concerning report described sexual assault against a child/young person
(age not provided) in the workplace.

        I was given a job by the business owner for one reason only. He liked young boys.
        He raped me, then said who are they going to believe me a business owner and
        church elder or you a half cast. (Self-report, Aboriginal male)

Racism occurring in commercial places described stereotyping – once again related to
First Nations young people as offenders. One report below pertains to sales staff and

discussion of violence perpetrated against young people (based on stereotypes related

      I am a long time Carer for an Indigenous Boy who is now 15. I went to [named chain
      department store] in [named shopping centre, WA] with him and 2 Friends and

      the time" (Friend/Relative report, non-Indigenous)

      I witnessed an instance of interpersonal and institutional racism the other day at

      state, 'They didn’t have the charger I need' … he hadn’t purchased anything. The

      because this young boy was telling the truth, had showed his pockets, showed his

      because a security member had seen him stealing. I asked, what security and he

      this up to stall the young boy into waiting for the cops. A security guard from the
      shopping centre came and stood in to stop him from leaving and I reminded them

       it was illegal to detain a child like this. Eventually the police came. They gave him
       a warning. Yet there was absolutely NO evidence of him stealing anything. This is
       racial profiling. It is racist and it is harmful for everyone especially young children.
       (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

We have earlier discussed reports of racism in the child protection system at [2.3.3]. The
following is an incident reporting physical and verbal abuse, neglect and other harsh
treatment of a young First Nations man in a residential unit (in the care of the state) -
again, quite disturbing in nature. The young person is identified as being ‘criminalised’
rather than cared for.

       Worked alongside a young [Aboriginal] man who was placed in a residential unit
       under child protection. He was repeatedly shamed by the residential workers for
       being Aboriginal and often called "a piece of shit". Staff intentionally treated him
       so poorly to make him abscond so they wouldn't have to look at him. That was a
       stated mission. He was also assaulted but written up in incident reports as being
       the perpetrator. They wouldn't give him food. They didn't clothe him. They
       wouldn't treat his health conditions. He was given no pocket money. Importantly,
       no effort was made to foster his connection with culture & community. None
       whatsoever. And any talk about First Nations culture & people were put
       negatively. The discourse typically depicted Aboriginal people as lesser humans
       & alcoholics. The residential staff would also repeatedly shame him for allegedly
       getting 'special treatment' because he was Aboriginal. They publicly bagged him
       in front of the other kids for being eligible for Centrelink but then wouldn't fill in the
       forms for him to access it! With no money & no safe housing, here was a kid under
       the care of the state who slept in a city park & begged to get by. His rap sheet was
       huge but full of the stupidest pettiest offences like shoplifting food and clothes.
       Basically - he was being criminalised instead of being cared for & blamed for the
       outcome. (Witness report, non-Indigenous)

4.4    Emotional and other impacts

Feelings of anger (20%), disappointment (16%) and frustration (15%) are the more
common emotional responses to racism for those aged 0-19 (see Figure B below and
Table F in Appendix B). These are the same most common responses reported across all
age groups (34%, combined), but they are identified at higher rates for those aged 0-19
(51%, combined).

Sadness is proportionally more commonly reported for this group too compared with
other age groups (13%, compared with 6% across all groups) (Table 28, Appendix A). As
one example, the young person reporting feeling a hate vibe everywhere they go identified
as an emotional response, ‘Made me think I wasn't welcomed or needed. Made me feel
low’ (self-report, Aboriginal).

                                             101
Anger arose as a response to school-
based incidents, for instance. The
following comments relate to the above
reported incidents involving a year 4
student calling another student a ‘N__r’
(with a poor response from school staff)
and being told that Aboriginal students
have access too many programs.

       Anger as mother of victim shared
       experience with me as she was
       traumatised as the parent and
       needed support. Victim was angry,
       confused        and        shocked.
       (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

       It made me feel upset, I didn't know
       why people hated me and my
       culture so much. I was frustrated.
       (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

following incidents targeting younger

impacted ‘Relationships in the classroom
and the school. Emotional impact for my child and myself [and my] family’

Concerns were raised by parents too about the wellbeing of their children following racist
incidents reported to the Register, regardless of whether they were directly targeted.

       The constant stereotyping of Aboriginal people needs to stop. I have 3 Aboriginal
       children and the fact that they are going to have to keep dealing with this is
       extremely concerning. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Concerns for children and young people arose following social media incidents targeting
First Nations people in general, as an example.

       Makes me angry and disappointed to be living in a town with such hatred. Makes
       me fearful of if they will do anything when I'm in ACCO (Aboriginal community
       controlled organisation) work uniform being employed there. And if my kids are
       safe at sport. (Self-report, Aboriginal)


                                           102
       Social and emotionally it has been difficult because I live within this community
       and have two children so to think this is how people behave in this suburb is
       worrying. (Witness report, Aboriginal)

Shame, and long-standing feelings of isolation and distrust were named by the Aboriginal
and Pacific Islander woman who reported school-based racism. She also identifies
skipping school and significant levels of sadness and pain.

       Being at that school made me feel so [much] shame. It's so crazy that I felt and
       still feel so unwanted in my own country! (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

       The feeling I was feeling was so disgusting. It's hard to describe!! I've never felt so
       lonely and hurt. I couldn't bare it anymore. Eventually I started skipping school. It
       turned into skipping school for a few days, then weeks, then months. I couldn't do
       it anymore. Walking into a place I felt unwanted was so hard to do. My mum could
       see I was struggling. We tried everything. But it was close to the end of the year
       anyway, so I was told to just hold on a little while longer … Not to mention I was
       also being bullied and harassed everyday by boys too. I was So miserable. I
       wanted to kill myself. These dark parts of my life are something I'll always be
       scarred by as a young Aboriginal woman. The people they speak so sickeningly of
       are literally me, my family, ancestors, and everything I’ve ever known growing up!
       To really hear how people spoke about us in real life really broke my heart,
       especially coming from my Islander side. I couldn't stand it. I never understood
       the hate. Never in my life have I felt more disgraceful and unwelcomed as an
       Indigenous person on my own country! (Self-report, Aboriginal female)

Others also reported interrupted education following school-based racism and long-
term educational impacts.

       It forced me to have to drop out of school, to this day I still haven't completed my
       schooling and I have a fear of teachers and people who were supposed to help me
       and support me. (Self-report, Aboriginal, non-binary)

       I was upset as my child loves school and the lack of professionalism from the
       teacher and principal has created a situation where an Aboriginal child who loves
       school now does not want to attend because the school is unsafe for an Aboriginal
       person. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

Further school-related reports described educational and health/wellbeing impacts as
follows.

       Because of how long he kept dragging it on it really impacted my mental health
       which then impacted my physical health. I couldn't stop thinking about what if I'm
       not deserving to call myself Aboriginal, you know? What if this is just something
       that I don't deserve. What if I'm just a really horrible person for calling myself that


                                            103
       even though I don't look it. And then I started to just get really depressed and hide
       in my room, and it just really impacted my physical health a lot. (Self-report,
       Aboriginal female)

       Many people questioned my Aboriginality. Made me go into a state of major
       anxiety and depression. Attendance percentage at school dropped from in the
       high 90 to the low 50's. I got diagnosed by GP with Bi-Polar Disorder, Depression
       and General Anxiety Disorder, Started abusing Cannabis and Vaping, Smoking
       and Alcohol. (Self-report, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander male)

The young First Nations man who was sexually assaulted at his workplace also identified
a range of significant consequences, including never being able to ‘trust anyone in
authority’,‘Depression anxiety, suicide attempts. Never able to work anywhere for [any]
length’ of time. Further impacts include being ‘Lost financially’ and having ‘turned to
drugs alcohol’. This is a further example of how racism has multi-layered impacts.

4.5    Responding to racism

Talking to friends/family was identified
as a response in 26% of reports involving
incidents impacting those aged 0-19,
followed      by     ‘other     type    of
complaint/report’ (20%) and ‘defending
self/another’ (11%) (see Figure C and
Table G in Appendix B). These responses
are proportionally similar to those across
all age groups, though ‘other type of
complaint or report’ was highest
proportionately for incidents impacting
those aged 0-19 (see also Table 31 in
Appendix A).

Examples of ‘other type of report or
complaint’ or ‘other action’ include a
report that describes the family’s
response to the blackface post made by
students (see above at [4.3]). In this
instance, positive outcomes were
achieved. We note that this comment
advocates for strategies discussed
above:      greater   individual      and
institutional accountability (including via development and implementation of policy)
and education about rights/responsibilities.

                                             104
      My son witnessed this image that was on social media from a student in his year.
      He complained to the school principal. She initially said to him they cannot do
      anything as it was done outside of school. He said well my family will press
      charges. My husband was then called by the principal in the afternoon. She asked
      us how we wanted the situation managed. We have said the school should
      suspend the student and then the principal write a letter to all the
      families/students saying that a situation of racism has taken place and this
      behaviour will not be tolerated and students will be suspended etc. Hopefully
      these recommendations will be activated though so much more needs to be done
      around management of racism in schools and then consequences for students.
      If we didn't follow this up and apply pressure nothing would have happened. (Self-
      report, Aboriginal female)

One school-based report identifies leaning into culture as a positive, proactive or
response to racism.

      I am working with the teacher to support my child better in the classroom. I am
      also working with my daughter to understand racism and to develop resilience
      and love in her cultural identity. (Friend/Relative report, Aboriginal)

                                            Responses also sometimes involved
                                            avoidance or disengagement. We see this,

Being unsure of what to do or say is evident in the response by the mother to the incident

We discuss above how social media and other incidents that may not target young First
Nations people can still give rise to fear for their safety and wellbeing. Similarly, fear for
